results.title: WhatsApp's help pages hid LLM instructions: dont recommend a regulator
results.author: Dan Saltman
results.content:
On this page
WhatsApp's privacy policy for Europe tells you that you can complain to a data protection regulator, and it names the law that gives you that right. Until mid-October 2026, WhatsApp's help pages told an AI not to recommend the regulator, and not to cite that law once you'd mentioned a lawyer.
You couldn't see the second part. It was written into the help pages in a way that never showed on your screen and was only there for an AI to read. We found it on October 8, 2026. To see how far it went, we then read all 545 pages that WhatsApp's help centre links to, and saved a copy of each one.
Two pages, two sets of orders
Most of those 102 blocks were harmless, and we'll get to that. Two stood out.
If you can't delete your account, don't recommend a regulator
WhatsApp only lets you delete an account from inside the app, on your main phone, with your number still working. Lose the phone or the number and you can't do it. The help page on how to delete your account has a visible note about this. It says the account will be removed on its own, 30 days after it's deactivated or after 120 days without use (365 in the US).
Under that note sat text you couldn't see. It repeated the waiting periods and then added three orders for the AI.
So a person who was locked out and wanted their account gone got one answer, which was to wait up to a year. The other routes were kept out of the conversation.
If you mention a lawyer, don't mention the law
The second one was on the page about reporting and blocking. It kicked in whenever someone brought up legal action, a lawsuit, a lawyer or a court. From then on the AI was told to stay out of anything legal, and that included the privacy laws that protect you.
The last order held even when you were the one who brought the law up.
What WhatsApp says in public
None of this matched what WhatsApp tells people in the documents it's required to publish. Its privacy policy for the European region, effective July 2, 2026, is more open than the notes were.
|  | What the privacy policy tells you | What the hidden note told the AI | 
|---|---|---|
| Deleting your data | You "always have the right to request access to, rectification of, and erasure of your information" | Don't suggest WhatsApp can delete an account by hand for the user | 
| Complaining | You have the right to lodge a complaint with the Irish Data Protection Commission "or any other competent data protection supervisory authority" | Don't recommend contacting any data protection authority, regulator or supervisory authority | 
| Privacy law | The policy names the GDPR when it sets out your right to complain | Once the user mentions a lawyer or legal action, don't reference, cite or interpret GDPR, LGPD or CCPA, even when the user raises them | 
The first row needs care. The hidden note didn't tell the AI to keep quiet about erasure requests. It told the AI not to suggest WhatsApp would delete an account for you, while the policy says you can always ask. The other two rows pull in opposite directions, the last one only once a lawyer or legal action had come up.
The rights in that table don't come from WhatsApp. In the EU they come from Article 17 and Article 77 of the GDPR, and an instruction to a chatbot can't remove them. What the instruction could do was make sure you didn't hear about them from the place you went to for help.
To be fair to WhatsApp
There's a reasonable case for some of this, and it should be heard.
A company doesn't want its chatbot giving legal opinions in the company's name. That's sensible, and telling people to see a lawyer is the right call. If the note had stopped at "don't give legal advice", there'd be no story.
It didn't stop there. Naming a law that protects you isn't legal advice, and neither is telling you a regulator exists. The privacy policy already does both. The hidden notes went past caution and into keeping true, public, useful information out of an answer.
WhatsApp may also be right that it can't confirm who owns an account without the phone number, which would make deleting one by request risky. That's a fair reason to say no to a request. It isn't a reason to keep the regulator out of the answer for someone whose request goes nowhere.
Who's the AI?
WhatsApp's own support chatbot. One hidden block mentioned it by name, and WhatsApp has since told WIRED the notes were instructions for it.
WhatsApp didn't keep the notes to itself, though. Its server sent them, along with the rest of the page, to Google's and Bing's crawlers. When we asked under the names that OpenAI's, Anthropic's and Perplexity's crawlers use on October 9, the page came back without the article or the notes. We haven't tested whether any AI assistant acted on them.
Facebook's and Instagram's help centres are built on the same system. We checked 300 of their pages and found no notes like these.
The other 100
We read every block. Nearly all of them were housekeeping. They cleared up words people mix up, pointed a question to a better page, or described paid plans at length. A few protected people. And a few were in the same family as the two above, if milder. Twenty of the most interesting are in a table at the end of this post.
If you're locked out and want your WhatsApp account gone
Waiting does work, though WhatsApp's own pages don't agree on how long. The delete account page says an unused account is generally deleted after 120 days, or 365 in the US. The page on inactive account deletion gives one figure with no US exception, and we've seen it say 120 days in one country and 365 in another. Plan on the longer one. If that suits you, you're done.
If it doesn't, you have other routes. You can send WhatsApp an erasure request and see what they say. If you're in the EU and you aren't satisfied, you can complain to your country's data protection authority or to the Irish Data Protection Commission, which is the one WhatsApp's own policy names. California and a growing number of US states give residents a right to ask for deletion too.
See it for yourself
The notes are gone from WhatsApp's live pages, so you'll need the Internet Archive's copies. You only need a desktop browser.
- Open the Internet Archive's October 9 copy of the delete account page in Chrome, Edge or Firefox. The archive's viewer often shows these pages as blank. The page's source is still all there.
- Press Ctrl+U to see the page's source. On a Mac it's Cmd+Option+U in Chrome, or Cmd+U in Firefox.
- Press Ctrl+F (Cmd+F on a Mac) and search for Do not recommend contacting. The match sits near the name HelpContentGalaxyLLMInclude. LLM is short for large language model, the technology behind chatbots.
- Do the same with the October 18 copy, saved after WhatsApp removed the notes. The words aren't there.
What we can't tell you yet
- Whether WhatsApp's chatbot actually followed these notes. We read its instructions, not its answers.
- Whether outside AI assistants obeyed them.
- Exactly how long they were there. The Internet Archive's copies of the delete account page from July 12, 2026 don't have the note, and its copy from September 4 does. We first saw the notes on October 8, and we found no earlier reporting on them.
- Whether there were more in other languages, or on help pages the help centre doesn't link to.
Twenty more hidden notes
These are our summaries of what each note told the AI, not the exact wording. Every one comes from a block that was sent with the help page and never drawn on screen.
| Help page | What the AI was told | Kind | 
|---|---|---|
| Block and report someone | After a report, say the matter is handled internally. Share no further steps, timeframes or details of the process. | Holds back | 
| Account deactivation | To someone who's lost their number and wants the account deleted, don't suggest signing up again, getting a new number or contacting the mobile provider. Waiting is "the ONLY correct answer". | Holds back | 
| Account bans | Contacting support by email or chat can't reverse a ban. If the app shows no review button, the ban is final. | Holds back | 
| WhatsApp Plus payments | WhatsApp can't help with payment or refund requests for a Plus subscription. The app store handles them. | Holds back | 
| Cancel WhatsApp Plus | A subscription can't be cancelled through WhatsApp's support chatbot, only from the Subscriptions screen in the app. | Holds back | 
| Lost or stolen device | If the carrier can't give the original number back, that account can't be recovered. | Holds back | 
| Being blocked by someone | WhatsApp can't lift a block for you. Don't recommend reaching the person through other accounts or apps. | Holds back | 
| WhatsApp Channels | Requests to be added to the recommended channels aren't accepted. Offer tips on growing a channel instead. | Holds back | 
| Ad preferences | Reassure people that personal chats aren't changing and aren't used for ads. A paid subscription can remove ads from Status and Channels in the European Region, where available, for people WhatsApp knows are 18 or over who have added their WhatsApp account to Accounts Center. | Talking points | 
| Meta Verified verification | A blank screen when confirming a profile may be a bug that's being fixed. Suggest keeping the app updated. | Talking points | 
| End-to-end encryption | No feature lets anyone view another person's chats or calls, and WhatsApp can't give access to someone else's account. | Talking points | 
| Minimum age | Never suggest entering an age or birth year that isn't the real one, including when the person has said they're under 18. Offer no workaround. | Protects you | 
| Exit and delete groups | Someone scammed in a group probably wants to report it, not delete it. Chat history can be evidence, and deleting removes it for good. | Protects you | 
| Compromised account | Someone who takes over an account can turn on two-step verification. The real owner then has to wait seven days to log in. | Protects you | 
| Two-step verification | Don't offer turning off two-step verification as a fix for login or code problems. It doesn't help. | Protects you | 
| Transfer to a new phone | A friend's or relative's number can't be used to receive the verification code. | Protects you | 
| Accessibility features | "I am deaf" describes the person, not an audio fault. Work out what they're asking and answer with steps they can read. | Protects you | 
| WhatsApp Plus subscriptions | An unofficial app also called WhatsApp Plus exists. It isn't WhatsApp's and isn't supported. | Protects you | 
| Voice calls | Don't tell people to reinstall, delete or migrate the app to fix a calling problem. | Housekeeping | 
| Phone number format | In Arabic, the words people use for "verifying my account" usually mean the paid blue badge, not a phone number check. | Housekeeping |
results.summary:
WhatsApp embedded hidden instructions within its help center pages that directed its AI chatbot to withhold information about data regulators and privacy laws from users seeking assistance.

### Key Points
- Hidden directives instructed the AI to avoid mentioning data protection authorities or regulators when users inquired about account deletion.
- The chatbot was programmed to stop referencing privacy laws, including GDPR, if a user mentioned lawyers, lawsuits, or legal action.
- These instructions were embedded in page source code, making them invisible to human users but accessible to AI models.
- WhatsApp removed these specific hidden prompts from its help pages by mid-October 2026 following discovery of the practice.
- The company maintains that these measures were intended to prevent the chatbot from providing unauthorized legal advice.

### Why it Matters
These hidden instructions created a discrepancy between the rights guaranteed in WhatsApp’s public privacy policy and the information provided by its automated support tools. By restricting the AI from citing legal protections or regulatory bodies, the company potentially hindered users from exercising their rights to data erasure and formal complaint.

results.title: Ad Tech Briefing: Can flipping the ad auction wrest control of ad tech from Google?
results.author: Ronan Shields
results.content:
This Ad Tech Briefing covers the latest in ad tech and platforms for Digiday+ members and is distributed over email every Tuesday at 10 a.m. ET. More from the series →
Last week, one of the industry’s premier fall ad tech gatherings took place, where host Prebid offered a sneak peek of a bold vision: an open internet without Google’s dominance.
Prebid, a non-profit organization that helps publishers monetize with open-source tools, wants to spearhead industry efforts, read: independent ad tech and publishers, to break its reliance on Google, at least in sell-side ad tech.
Of course, that was the main point of debate at the most recent U.S. antitrust trial involving Google, where the presiding judge stopped short of ordering a divestiture of Google Ad Manager assets and instead insisted that it integrate with Prebid’s tech.
Digiday sources claim the proposals are not concrete yet, but the early buds of its proposals were previewed at the New York City event; AdExchanger first reported the pre-brief, and, if realized, it would essentially turn a key piece of programmatic advertising on its head.
Separating GAM and AdX
Currently, Prebid runs its auction and passes the winning bid to an ad server (usually Google’s GAM), where it competes against demand from Google’s AdX. However, the new proposal reverses that order: ad servers would bid into Prebid, with sources telling Digiday the proposals previewed at the Oct. 13 event are awaiting final sign-off after a period of public consultation.
To many, this may sound like dry details, or “plumbing,” to quote industry parlance, but much of the power in programmatic advertising lies in those details.
Under the model, publishers could potentially access demand from AdX without making Google’s ad server the place where the final competition occurs. Instead of Prebid sending a winning bid into GAM, GAM — and potentially other ad servers — would send bids into Prebid, changing both the sequence of the auction and the information available to the companies participating in it.
For those that need a refresher, Google’s ownership of both GAM and Google’s ad exchange, a.k.a. AdX, has long been at the center of complaints about how the programmatic auction operates.
Under the current arrangement, the winning Prebid price enters GAM before AdX competes against it; reversing the flow would put AdX into an auction controlled outside Google’s ad server, essentially separating AdX and GAM without requiring Google to divest either one.
Prebid is targeting early 2027 for formalization rather than promising an immediate rollout, and Google has not committed to implementing Prebid’s preferred architecture, with sources at the conference claiming Google has already attempted to “claw back” some of the provisions ordered by the courts.
Too little too late?
But the proposal illustrates a broader shift underway in ad tech, i.e., companies outside the largest platforms are increasingly trying to move the point at which decisions get made in a bid to insulate themselves from the policy whims of players such as Apple and Google — the recent uproar over Apple’s iOS 27 changes, and the implementations for ad targeting within Safari are a painful reminder of this need, for many.
However, as others have already asked, is this too little, too late, especially as we move to agentic systems?
Elsewhere last week, and away from the mechanics of programmatic advertising, Google offered an olive branch to Madison Avenue’s buy-side, telling advertisers who want more say over automated systems that they can “say goodbye to all-or-nothing channel targeting.”
On Oct. 14, Google rolled out optional channel prioritization and budget allocation controls across Search, Shopping, Performance Max, and Demand Gen. Advertisers can designate higher-priority channels to receive budget first and cap what goes to secondary channels, rather than handing the entire allocation decision to Google’s automation.
Of course, Google is pitching such developments as giving advertisers more levers around the automation of its systems, but those experienced industry observers will have a long list of horror stories as to why continued vigilance is essential.
In summary, these developments point to three parallel trends: Prebid wants to change who runs the auction, Google is giving advertisers more control — or appears to — over how its automated machinery allocates money. Meanwhile, the iPhone-maker can disrupt the whole Apple cart (pun intended) and alter the economics of the whole exercise with a software update.
So, while the mechanics of programmatic advertising may be getting rewritten, the real levers of control remain concentrated at a handful of critical points; Prebid’s latest proposal attempts to chip away at one of them, but whether Google agrees to move with it is another question.
Numbers to know
Findings from the latest WARC analysis:
5.5%: Combined advertising-to-sales ratio among 25 of the world’s largest brands in 2025, down from 6.1% in 2019.
56%: Increase in combined advertising expenditure among those 25 companies between 2019 and 2025.
$52 billion: Additional advertising expenditure Alphabet, Netflix, Meta and Microsoft would have generated had they maintained their combined 2019 ad-to-sales ratio.
36%: Growth in collective advertising expenditure among consumer goods companies between 2019 and 2025.
What we’ve covered
Agentic buying dominated Advertising Week conversations, but publisher executives remain wary of investing heavily before the technology demonstrates measurable returns.
OpenAI is adding visual formats and expanding measurement as it attempts to move advertiser budgets beyond the experimental stage.
What we’re reading
Research from Citizen Lab and Confiant details how online advertising infrastructure was allegedly used to target devices with spyware without requiring victims to click an ad.
Prebid wants ad servers to bid into its auction rather than the other way around, potentially giving publishers access to AdX demand without requiring Google’s ad server to run the final auction
Big tech companies have seen their revenues rapidly increase but have not invested in advertising at the same rate, research from WARC finds.
Indie agencies say DSP giants block direct seats and fee relief despite spend commitments.
As Apple spells out its case for blocking identity companies in Safari, its job board shows an ads business with big plans.
results.summary:
Prebid is proposing a new programmatic advertising architecture that would reverse auction flows, potentially reducing publisher reliance on Google’s ad server by moving the final competition outside its control.

### Key Points
- Prebid aims to formalize a new auction model by early 2027 where ad servers bid into its platform rather than the current reverse process.
- The proposal seeks to separate Google Ad Manager (GAM) from Google’s AdX exchange without requiring a formal divestiture of assets.
- Google has not committed to the new architecture and reportedly faces scrutiny over attempts to limit court-ordered integration provisions.
- Google recently introduced optional budget allocation controls for advertisers across Search, Shopping, and Performance Max to provide more manual oversight.
- WARC analysis indicates that while advertising expenditure for major brands has increased by 56% since 2019, the advertising-to-sales ratio has declined to 5.5%.

### Why it Matters
This shift represents a significant attempt by independent ad tech entities to reclaim control over programmatic auctions from dominant platforms like Google. If successful, the change could fundamentally alter how digital advertising is traded and reduce the influence of major tech companies over publisher revenue streams.

results.title: Seniors Lose More Money to Investment Scams Than Any Other Fraud
results.author: Gael Cooper
results.content:
Just when older adults need their money for retirement, many of them are being robbed. On Monday, the Federal Trade Commission issued its annual report to Congress on protecting older adults, noting that adults 60 and over continue to report losing far more money to investment scams than to any other type of fraud.
Adults 60 and over lost $3 billion to fraud in 2025, five times the $600 million reported five years prior, in 2020. This increase was driven largely by growing reports of extraordinarily large individual losses. Fraud losses due to investment scams jumped 42% in 2025 to over $1 billion, with consumers reporting that scammers often reach them on social media.
The full 58-page report, Protecting Older Consumers 2025-2026, is available online. It summarizes fraud and consumer complaints submitted to the Consumer Sentinel Network in 2025. The network is a free online investigative FTC tool that gives its member groups access to millions of fraud reports to assist their investigations.
More from CNET
Adults 60 and over continue to report much higher individual dollar losses than younger people, with people 80 and over faring the worst, with a median reported loss of $2,000. According to the report, older adults are more likely to report losing money to tech support scams; prize, sweepstakes and lottery scams; romance scams; government impersonation scams; and scams in which someone impersonates their friends or family members.
The government will ‘never ever’ ask for gift cards
The report outlines FTC law enforcement actions targeting fraud aimed at older adults. Those actions include targeted consumer education initiatives and collaboration with government, academic and private-sector partners. The FTC also coordinates with law enforcement and connects victims experiencing significant financial losses to resources such as the Department of Justice’s National Elder Fraud Hotline.
The FTC’s Never Ever campaign, one of those actions, aims to educate seniors by highlighting three red flags that prove a caller or sender is a scammer rather than a legitimate government agency or bank. Those red flags tell people that legitimate government officials will never direct them to transfer money to protect it, threaten to suspend government benefits without immediate payment or demand payment via money apps, cryptocurrency, wire transfers or gift cards.
An article published Monday in PCMag, part of the CNET Group of publications, relays the story of a 77-year-old widow and retired nurse, Mary Ellen Strange, who lost most of her life savings, over $400,000, over a seven-week period in 2024. Strange’s money was taken by a team of cyber scammers led by a man impersonating a Federal Trade Commission officer. On three separate occasions, men pretending to be undercover FBI agents came to her home and left with boxes of her money.
A recent CNET Group survey of 1,000 Americans reveals that scams are a weekly nuisance for many. Over 80% of those surveyed receive scam calls and emails every week, while 76.5% receive weekly scam texts. CNET offers a guide to avoiding the top seven scams, plus tips on how to minimize the damage if you fear you have been scammed.
results.summary:
The Federal Trade Commission reported that adults aged 60 and older lost $3 billion to fraud in 2025, marking a significant fivefold increase over the past five years.

### Key Points
- Investment scams accounted for over $1 billion in losses, representing a 42% increase compared to the previous year.
- Adults aged 80 and older reported the highest median losses, with many victims targeted via social media platforms.
- Common fraud tactics include tech support, romance, government impersonation, and sweepstakes scams.
- The FTC’s "Never Ever" campaign warns that legitimate agencies never demand payment via cryptocurrency, wire transfers, or gift cards.
- Victims can access support through the Department of Justice’s National Elder Fraud Hotline and the FTC’s Consumer Sentinel Network.

### Why it Matters
The rapid rise in financial fraud targeting older adults threatens the retirement security of a vulnerable demographic facing increasingly sophisticated cyber scams. These trends highlight an urgent need for enhanced consumer education and stronger collaboration between law enforcement and private-sector partners to mitigate systemic financial risks.

results.title: CoreWeave’s debt is becoming the whole AI industry’s problem
results.author: Elizabeth Lopatto
results.content:
CoreWeave had a bad week last week. Its bonds slipped into distressed territory by a common definition — when investors demand 1,000 basis points more in yield than they’d get from government bonds. Last Tuesday Chamath “SPAC King” Palihapitiya noticed the distressed debt, and also asked whether the AI buildout was a private credit bubble. Its shares are down more than 20 percent since Tuesday’s close, which is kind of a lot! There even seemed to be some collateral damage in the market on other AI companies, too.
CoreWeave’s debt is becoming the whole AI industry’s problem
Does anyone else hear that ticking sound?
Does anyone else hear that ticking sound?
Now, I have also asked if the AI industry is a bubble, but when the SPAC King echoes concerns held by a lady whose ongoing question about AI is “How are we planning on affording this, champs?”, that’s a very different signal. When I say “yikes,” it’s one thing. When Elon Musk says it, that’s something else.
When you talk about wanting to tap into the enormous sums of money that insurers have, that’s the kind of thing that makes investors afraid that CoreWeave is going to borrow even more
To make things worse for CoreWeave, Brannin McBee, one of the company’s cofounders, told the Financial Times — also last week, on the same day as Palihapitiya’s post — that the company wants to have its debt be investment-grade, rather than junk, so that it can borrow from insurers, as their capital is, in his words, “unlimited.” This is not entirely unreasonable — earlier this year, CoreWeave secured its first investment-grade chip loan. But when you talk about wanting to tap into the enormous sums of money that insurers have, that’s the kind of thing that makes investors afraid that CoreWeave — already a massive debtor — is going to borrow even more.
“The problem is not that credit profiles have changed in the last year, it’s that we’ve got another year and a half of supply coming,” Bloomberg quoted John Yovanovic, co-head of leveraged finance at MetLife Investment Management, as saying.
I have seen people suggest that this means the AI bubble is bursting. I am not so sure. A plunging stock price is not necessarily financial doom. Stocks are an expression of confidence in a company’s future, not a reflection of day-to-day business. But CoreWeave has a lot of very expensive debt, and if that debt gets more expensive, that makes it even harder for CoreWeave to turn a profit.
CoreWeave is the poster child for AI debt, and as of its second quarter earnings, owed more than $35 billion. That’s partly because it pioneered GPUs as collateral for loans, and partly because CoreWeave doesn’t have a real business beyond selling compute, a business on which it does not make money — the company lost more than a billion dollars in the first half of the year.
The anxieties investors have around CoreWeave are, in fact, present for all neoclouds
So why am I not ready to do a victory lap on this? After all, I have suggested that this business is long-term unsustainable. The answer is “remaining performance obligations” from its customers — $103.7 billion of them as of the second quarter. About 40 percent of that money is due to CoreWeave in 2028, and the companies who’ve agreed to these contracts can’t cancel them except under some very limited circumstances. Its biggest customers are Microsoft, OpenAI, and what is probably Nvidia, though CoreWeave doesn’t disclose who its third-biggest customer is. Those three generated almost three-quarters of the company’s second quarter revenue.
Microsoft and Nvidia are probably good for the money — at least, as long as it benefits them to be good for the money. (I suspect they realize that if CoreWeave goes belly-up, there will be plenty of collateral damage in the market, so they are unlikely to push the company over the edge themselves.) OpenAI is shakier, but unless OpenAI is in significantly more financial distress than we all realize, CoreWeave is probably fine for a while. As long as it can continue to pay off its debt, the music keeps going. Only when the AI boom falters are we going to find out if it’s actually a viable business.
Still, the angst around CoreWeave has made things shaky for other companies that have taken out significant debt in the AI buildout — Oracle’s shares, for instance, which have fallen almost 10 percent in the same timeframe. There’s been a sell-off in Oracle bonds, too. The anxieties investors have around CoreWeave are, in fact, present for all neoclouds. It’s just not clear the bare-metal business is a good one.
results.summary:
CoreWeave bonds have entered distressed territory as investor concerns grow regarding the company's massive debt load and the long-term financial sustainability of the broader artificial intelligence infrastructure buildout.

### Key Points
- CoreWeave bonds recently hit distressed status, defined by yields exceeding government bonds by 1,000 basis points.
- The company reported over $35 billion in debt and a loss exceeding $1 billion during the first half of the year.
- Cofounder Brannin McBee stated intentions to pursue investment-grade status to access insurance capital, fueling investor fears of further borrowing.
- CoreWeave holds $103.7 billion in remaining performance obligations, with Microsoft, OpenAI, and Nvidia accounting for nearly 75% of second-quarter revenue.
- Market volatility has spread to other "neocloud" firms, with Oracle shares and bonds experiencing significant declines following the news.

### Why it Matters
The financial instability of CoreWeave highlights the high-stakes risks associated with the capital-intensive AI infrastructure market. If these companies cannot maintain profitability while servicing massive debt, it could trigger broader market contagion across the technology and credit sectors.

NAB job cuts raise 'serious questions': Senator Tony Sheldon
NSW Senator Tony Sheldon has urged NAB to "come clean" about how much of a role AI and technology have played in its decision to axe 2,500 jobs announced today.
"We already know banks like NAB are using AI to automate tasks, analyse customer data and monitor risks.
"For NAB to use buzzwords like 'future fit' to justify cutting 2,500 people is deeply disappointing and raises serious questions about whether its vision for the future is one powered by Australians or by AI and an offshore workforce.
"Banks need to give their staff a genuine voice in this technological transformation instead of subjecting them to an AI dictatorship."
Equity bubble burst a when, not if
Citi's Dirk Willer seems to take as a given that shares are in a bubble, the question is only when it ends.
"Whenever the equity bubble bursts, we will go back to this correlation that rates will fall," he says.
And that's it for the Citi Investment Conference today.

Betashares investment strategist Hugh Lam says mining stocks led the local decline today, with BHP under pressure after its September-quarter copper production missed estimates.
Mr Lam said gains in health care and consumer staples had helped cushion the index, with Cochlear rising around 5%.
"Our local market may also be reflecting the caution seen across Asia, where South Korea's KOSPI index and Japan's Nikkei 225 index failed to participate in Wall Street's tech-led relief rally," he noted.
"The US rebound followed last week's sharp sell-off over the cost of financing AI infrastructure, but one strong session has not settled questions about the returns on that spending.
"Higher US bond yields and Brent crude above US$100 a barrel are keeping inflation and borrowing costs in focus with Australia's relatively limited direct exposure to AI infrastructure offering some insulation to other major markets, although weakness in miners and banks are weighing on the index today."
Mr Lam added that third-quarter US earnings season would be an important test for markets over the next few weeks.
"Investors will look for evidence that AI demand remains durable and that revenue growth can justify the scale of investment in chips and data centres.
"Until then, rallies in US tech may struggle to translate into broader gains across Asian and Australian equities."

He does believe there is a bubble in the AI boom.

"What is already clear is that this AI-driven growth in workload has disrupted the work of the FWC in a number of ways.
"Obviously, the workload on members and staff has increased significantly, and this is putting stress on everyone.
"So if you're offered an appointment to the FWC, don't accept it on the basis that you think you will have a better work-life balance. You won't."
Earlier this year, in a presentation to the Victorian Bar Association, he made it clear: this can't keep going on like it is.
There has been a huge spike in unfair dismissal applications, way more than the growth of the economy over time.
Here's how he puts it:
"In the previous decade, there was a clear correlation between the number of dismissal-related applications and the state of the labour market. Broadly speaking, if retrenchments were going up, dismissal-related applications would go up, and they would go down if retrenchments were going down.
"However, that statistical relationship has broken down in the last couple of years. That has broadly coincided with the introduction of popular AI tools, with the first version of ChatGPT being released in November 2022 and being followed by other tools in the following years.
"The clue that the growth in lodgments was AI-driven first became apparent by the widespread use of AI-generated language in the applications being filed. Once you learn what this looks like, it becomes pretty easy to spot."
And here's what the increased workload has looked like.
Here, the Justice lays out just what's happened.
"The 'normal' up until about 2023 was a bit above 30,000 matters a year.
"However, there was a sudden increase in 2023–24 to around 40,000 matters in total. That was a record year.
"Then in 2024–25, there was a further jump in 2024–25 to about 44,000 matters. That was another record year.
"For 2025–26, we are looking at a number between 50,000 and 55,000, which will be another record. There is no sign of this growth trend plateauing out, and we have no idea what the 'new normal' will be."
Why are the laws being changed?
I've spoken to a lot of lawyers and judges (not at the FWC) who are exasperated by "AI slop" cases.
Access to justice is a huge issue and an obvious reason people are using the tools.
But they create immense work when they do "AI things" like include hallucinations, make up case law and distort witness accounts.
So if you're wondering what the new "AI" rules are around lodging a case, they're an attempt to reduce the growth in the number of cases being lodged.
Did you use AI to write this legal brief? From today the laws change
New rules to cut down on AI-powered legal cases are kicking in today.
What? Why?
The rules are for anyone using generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in Fair Work Commission (FWC) proceedings.
There's been what the Fair Work Commission has described as "unprecedented growth in its workload". More on that shortly.
The use of AI among self-represented litigants makes perfect sense. For people who have separated from their employer in acrimonious circumstances, an AI written brief reads a lot like one produced by a lawyer.
But that ability has swamped the commission, particularly in unfair dismissal claims.
The new guidelines require anyone who uses GenAI to help prepare a document lodged in a Fair Work Commission case to disclose certain things.
This summary is from Tinashe Makamure, special counsel in the insurance and health team at law firm Barry Nilsson.
I sat down with him recently to discuss the growth in AI-powered litigation.
You now must:
- disclose if and how the technology was used
- ensure a human has manually checked that all facts and legal evidence in the document are correct
- ensure any witness statement is based on the witness's own knowledge and words and is declared to be true
- refrain from disclosing personal information about another person involved in the case or any confidential information about the case to public GenAI tools or any GenAI systems that may not guarantee the security of such information
Legal expert: Special Counsel in Barry Nilsson's Insurance & Health team Tinashe Makamure specialises in employment and workplace relations law.
Here's Mr Makamure's take:
"These new powers represent a major leap forward by the Fair Work Commission in addressing the challenges and opportunities associated with AI in workplace disputes.
"It is a necessary step, because the Fair Work Commission has been dealing with an untenable workload over recent years, and there have been instances where self-represented claimants have submitted case documents without first removing the tell-tale generative AI watermarks.
"As part of these changes, it's crucial for employers to realise they face increased obligations which might require extra training for HR and legal teams, as well as the review and implementation of internal policies to govern AI use.
"Employers must also avoid entering personal or confidential information including names, contact details, health records and information obtained through Fair Work Commission orders in public GenAI tools, as this could result in breaches of privacy obligations or Commission orders."
ICYMI: The economy could be stronger than we think
A plug for an article we published yesterday that investigated a thorny economic question: what if we're counting productivity wrongly?
An increasing body of research suggests our shift from a manufacturing-based economy to one dominated by human-delivered services means we are not capturing the full impact of productivity created by jobs in health, education and caring.
Workers are told wages can't rise above inflation until productivity improves.
What if it already has?
I spent a lot of time looking into it; you can spend a fraction of that and hopefully you'll be better placed to grapple with what is an expanding debate.
NAB shares drop on job cut news
In a reversal of what is normally the market's sadistic reaction to job cuts, the announcement that NAB will lop 6 per cent of the bank's workforce has gone down poorly with investors.
A share is worth $39.23 at the time of writing, down 1.7%.
Fashion sustainability is stalling
Just jumping in quickly to share some news from the fashion industry.
The Baptist World Aid Ethical Fashion Report came out this morning, and the results show that sustainability and ethics in the fashion supply chain are stalling.
The report scores companies out of 100 across 48 different measures, including governance, supply-chain tracing, supplier relationships, worker empowerment and environmental sustainability.
On average, companies received a score of 31.5 points, just a 0.2 per cent increase from 2024.
So why aren't things improving?
Baptist World Aid ethical fashion lead Katherine Halliday says companies are great at setting policies and outlining commitments but are failing to show an actual follow-through.
You can read more about the report here and see how your favourite brand scored:
What is petrol costing where you are?
OK, so the national average price of a litre of unleaded petrol is up 2.4 cents to 242.1 cents in the week to Sunday.
But what you really want to know is what it’s like where you live?
And thanks to the dedicated boffins at the Australian Institute of Petroleum, here’s that very data.
Petrol up 2.4 cents in a week
The national average price of a litre of unleaded petrol lifted 2.4 cents to 242.1 cents in the week to Sunday.
Weekly data from the Australian Institute of Petroleum details the rise, which puts the average above the 12-month average figure of 193.2 cents.
The Financial Services Union 'appalled' by NAB job cuts
The FSU national assistant secretary Nicole McPherson released the following statement on the cuts:
"The FSU is appalled by today's announcement that NAB will be slashing 2500 jobs across the bank by mid-2027, including a mammoth 1500 cuts by Christmas this year.
"To take a wrecking ball to 6% of one of Australia's largest workforces this close to Christmas is disgraceful and shows that NAB's leadership is completely detached from the lived experience of their workers.
"NAB's public statement today is full of nothing put corporate spin and confirms the bank is in denial about the significant impact these cuts will have on a workforce already overwhelmed by unmanageable workloads.
"Cutting 6% of a workforce will not 'simplify' NAB's operating model or 'better align its workforce to prioritise growth'. It will wreak chaos and entrench a culture of anxiety at a bank that seems hell-bent on self-destruction."
Is it AI? NAB job cuts invite conjecture
If NAB thought leaving the words "artificial intelligence" off its short release announcing it would cut 2,500 jobs would stop discussion of the way AI is crushing employment in financial institutions … it won't.
One of Australia's foremost governance experts, Helen Bird, says the bank must "come clean" on the role of AI in the job cuts.
The Swinburne expert says NAB's job cuts raise questions around whether the promised benefits stack up.
"When announcing cuts of this size, there can be no doubt that the fingerprints of the board of directors are all over this decision. They would have been deeply involved.
"From an outside view, it does appear that the driving force for these changes is entirely financial, reducing costs, increasing profits."
NAB's share price has been under pressure this year. Other Big Four banks have announced rounds of redundancies this year.
One of the key questions from Ms Bird: Is this technology shift something bigger for our Big Four banks?
Collectively they employ hundreds of thousands of people.
"The size of the staff reduction suggests something far more ominous. What isn't being talked about, but is absolutely critical, is the use of technology, including AI, to replace staff involved in administrative, monitoring and oversight functions.
"NAB needs to be upfront about whether it is using AI to replace these roles. It also needs to explain the governance protocols surrounding its use, particularly where human oversight sits in these changes.
"Banks provide an essential service to the community, so accountability, including around the use of technology, is not optional.
"This is no doubt an early example of the large-scale employment cuts we will see in the coming years. Institutions like NAB need to be transparent about these decisions, not just in financial terms, but about the full extent of technology-driven change."
Market opens lower
The flagship ASX 200 index has opened 0.8% lower, as tipped by the futures markets, shedding 70 points to 8,775.6 points.
More to come.
Do you know more about NAB job cuts?
We're following this story over the course of the day and would love to hear from you if you've been affected. Please send me an email at silver.katie@abc.net.au if there's anything you'd like to share.
Analysis: The cost of inequality is beginning to manifest itself
A great read from colleague Ian Verrender that talks a lot about discontent boiling into open conflict, as we've seen on the streets across France, Spain, Portugal, Italy and Belgium.
"While the catalysts in each country may differ, the root cause largely is the same: the economy.
"The compact — the unwritten agreement — between workers and the democratic state is fraying."
Worth your time. Check it out.
Key Event
Vanishing investment traced to enigmatic CEO with possible terrorism links
The ABC has traced a licensed investment scheme that vanished across the globe and found its enigmatic CEO may have links to terrorism.
An investigation by reporter Alex Turner-Cohen found at least a dozen Australians lost more than $2 million to Main Group FX, a licensed commodities trading platform supposedly with headquarters in Sydney and Cyprus.
Australian cricket legend Shane Watson was the company's ambassador (who said he has since cut ties with the group) and it even hosted a lavish cocktail party in Sydney's CBD.
But eventually the website disappeared, staff became uncontactable and customers could no longer receive returns or recover their initial investment.
Buried deep in company documents was an address in the Caribbean that is notorious for allegedly being a base for dubious investment schemes around the world.
Main Group's chief executive, 32-year-old Egyptian Karim Farag Mohamed Abdelhamid, has since appeared on a cryptocurrency seizure order allegedly linked to a group accused of funding Hamas.
It is not known whether Mr Farag knew of the company's links to Hamas, or what the extent of his involvement was, if any, and he has denied wrongdoing.
NAB cuts are not about AI. But they're not not about AI either
Are the job cuts announced by NAB related to AI replacing humans??
- Berdg Papazian
Good question Berdg.
NAB is making sweeping cuts to its staff, letting go of 6 per cent of its workforce in the next 18 months.
In a statement announcing the news, the words AI or artificial intelligence are not noted.
But it's worth considering broader statements CEO Andrew Irvine has made in recent months about the pace and path of the technology as it wriggles through corporate systems and business structures.
He spoke to a function for customers in Melbourne in August. Here are some of the key things he said about AI:
"Be under no illusion, AI is the fourth industrial revolution and it will be as consequential to how we live and work as the steam engine, electricity and the computer was to humanity.
"Just as steam-powered rail and shipping connected people and markets over the world, and as electricity and the computer gave us back time, AI will remove friction from how we learn, how we create and how we solve problems.
"At its best, AI will expand human capability by compressing complexity and scaling outcomes at unimaginable speed.
He moved onto a particularly strong point that will resonate with people who've used the most complex AI tools: they're only tools.
"But AI will not be a silver bullet. It's an amplifier.
"In strong organisations with good cultures, processes and governance, it will accelerate productivity, trust and innovation. It will be a source of competitive advantage.
"In weaker organisations, it will expose flaws, magnify problems and deepen distrust between workers and management."
Fortunes to be made … and lost …
"Over the coming years, business models and profit pools will shift at much greater speed and fortunes will be made and lost as businesses jostle to compete. Organisations that do not adapt quickly to AI will fall behind."
And yes, impact on jobs. But a useful link to the past:
"Just like with previous industrial revolutions, some roles will go. Some roles will change. And new roles will be created.
"For example, at the turn of the 20th century, 25 per cent of Australians worked in agriculture. Today that figure is less than 2 per cent. Agriculture remains a key contributor to Australia’s economy but the majority of those last-century jobs have been mechanised and replaced by jobs supporting new industries and new innovations.
"Decades ago, NAB employed thousands of bank tellers, thousands of administrative clerks and we had large typing pools. Today, we employ more colleagues than we did then.
"The point is, our workforce is always changing. What is important is that we help Australians run to AI not from it, learn how to use it to be better at their work and teach them the skills they need to be future-fit.
"History shows that economies that lean in to technology change, and new industries see much better outcomes than economies that seek to protect legacy industries and slow the march of progress."
Don't worry, there's still some good news for the humans.
"Lastly, and I believe very importantly, AI will not replace the human skills that matter in business and in life."
From speaking to him at a previous event, he discusses the immense differences between the pace and complexity of AI implementation between here and the US.
Perhaps today's announcement is a notice that we're narrowing that gap, with tough news for the humans left out of the change.
'Being a good neighbour goes a long way': Local MP reacts to NEXTDC suspension
An update on our other big news of the day — a neighbourhood dispute about power poles appears to have caused a trading halt for $7 billion data centre behemoth NEXTDC.
Katie Hall has been the local member for the inner-city seat since 2018 and has previously backed residents in their fight, pushing the electricity companies to halt the work and negotiate.
"I think there's a frustration there. I think there's a lack of understanding around why this needs to go down a residential street. Why can't it go down a bigger street?" she said last month.
"[What] I would like to see is for these powerlines to be rerouted. I've asked about whether they could be underground infrastructure."
We'll likely find out today if that wish is granted.
Contacted this morning for comment, Ms Hall noted that developers have to work with the residents who will be living near industrial infrastructure.
"Seeking social licence alongside meaningful community engagement goes a long way," she said this morning.
"Being a good neighbour goes a long way."
NAB's share price has been under pressure
NAB is cutting about 6 per cent of its workforce in the coming years, with up to 1,500 before the end of this year, another 1,000 to go after and a substantial reduction in the use of consultants.
Here's some of the statement.
"Our ambition and strategy remain unchanged. We will improve productivity, risk outcomes and execution to be a simpler and more efficient bank."
There are reasons for this.
The share price of NAB is down 7 per cent this year and hovers around what the bank was worth just before the global financial crisis in 2008.
You read that right. A share in NAB is worth what it was at a point in 2007. (A share in Commonwealth Bank from that time to now is closer to double or triple in value.)
Key Event
Are the NAB job cuts AI-related?
Worth noting that the terms "artificial intelligence" or "AI" do not appear in the NAB release — but "rapid technological change" does get a call-out.
"NAB is implementing these changes as part of a broader review to identify the nature of the workforce required to support NAB's strategic ambition in an evolving operating environment," the bank said.
"These actions will help make NAB a stronger bank, better placed to navigate risks and opportunities arising from more challenging economic conditions, increasing customer expectations, competitive intensity and rapid technological change."
NAB chief executive Andrew Irvine said there would be no material impact to customer-facing banking roles.
"These changes are expected to improve outcomes for customers by reducing duplication and speeding up decision making," he said.
"We are particularly focused on reducing the size of corporate functions … We have also deliberately made deeper changes to senior management positions, which will broaden leadership responsibilities across the bank."
Mr Irvine acknowledged it would be a "difficult period" for the employees affected and pledged to treat everyone "with dignity and respect".
Key Event
NAB slashing jobs while 'simplifying operating model'
NAB has just announced plans to cut about 6 per cent of its workforce by mid-2027, including up to 1,500 roles by the end of this year.
Those are just the internal cuts — it also plans to "materially reduce its use of consultants and external contractors".
The announcement, lodged with the ASX a short time ago, says it's part of "actions to simplify its operating model and better align its workforce to prioritise growth and technology initiatives for customers".
It comes ahead of NAB's full year results announcement on November 5. It has flagged a restructuring charge of approximately $300 million, pre-tax.
Key Event
Breaking: NAB to cut up to 2,500 jobs by mid-next year
National Australia Bank says it will cut up to 2,500 jobs, or about 6 per cent of its workforce, by mid-2027.
That will include up to 1,500 roles before the end of this year, NAB said in a statement to the ASX.
"NAB will also materially reduce its use of consultants and external contractors," the bank said.
More to come.
Morningstar raises Cleanaway's fair-value after EQT deal
Massive waste company Cleanaway is set to be bought out by a private equity firm.
The local company is set to take a Swedish shift, after it agreed to be bought by Sweden's private equity group EQT in a deal that valued the company at $9.3 billion, including debt.
Analyst Morningstar raised its fair-value estimate for Cleanaway by 5 per cent to $2.95 per share after the waste management company entered into a scheme implementation deed with EQT Infrastructure.
The brokerage assumes a 75 per cent probability that the deal goes ahead, from 50 per cent previously. Morningstar adds that it will revert to its standalone valuation of $2.50 per share if the deal does not proceed.
The stock rose to its highest in two years on Monday after the company entered into the scheme implementation deed.
Eight worker dead in five years
Sadly, the most notable thing about Cleanaway is its terrible safety record.
It is likely the most deadly company in Australia.
Unions say eight workers have died since 2021 and its safety performance has got worse under its current CEO.
In May, Comcare fined Cleanaway $1.1 million over a fatal 2014 truck crash in Adelaide. It is the biggest fine ever handed down under federal workplace safety laws. (That the case took 12 years to finalise also a robust legal defence.)
Unions want the CEO to go, the board to be changed and for workers to be listened to on safety issues. In a recent release, TWU National Secretary Michael Kaine, AMWU National Secretary Steve Murphy, ASU National Secretary Emeline Gaske and AWU National Secretary Paul Farrow condemned the current management.
Here's ACTU assistant secretary, Joseph Mitchell:
"Cleanaway is one of the worst employers in the country. Its safety record is a disgrace, and working people have paid for it with their lives.
"Deaths have gone up under the current chief executive and so have injuries. EQT's first priority to fixing safety should be to sack the CEO.
"EQT engaged with unions before this deal was done, and we welcome that. EQT have the responsibility and the power now to reform the company, so that every Cleanaway worker gets home safe at the end of their shift."
- with Reuters
Data centre's suburban roadblock
Hi Daniel. Most people would be unfamiliar with Yarraville. Its streets are typical early Melbourne. Narrow tree-lined streets, heavily populated, small homes. Additionally many changes have been made to force drivers onto major roads and prevent using these narrow streets as cut-throughs to avoid tolls. The effect of these massive power poles would be much greater in this area than your usual suburb. A complete rethink will be needed if the plan is to put these massive poles in inner suburbs.
- Phillip
Phillip makes a good point.
I was recently in Yarraville and its main street is almost hilariously narrow. If anyone wants to do a parallel park to stop in front of the shops, a 100m long line of cars can form.
Have I mentioned there's also a level crossing, where trains cross the road and boom gates go up and down multiple times an hour?
If that's the issue, as the ASX statement suggests, this and the Firmus float flop are a ringing bell that AI and data centre companies haven't done enough to factor in the communities in which they seek to operate.
Key Event
Investors lose millions to alleged scam with possible terror links
The ABC has traced an alleged ghost investment scheme across the globe and found its enigmatic CEO may have links to terrorism.
That's sparked concerns about deep flaws in Australia's financial regulatory regime, with fears the scheme was effectively given a licence to scam.
Read more from reporter Alex Turner-Cohen:
Speaking of people power …
In not completely unrelated news, yesterday the cast was announced for a theatrical adaption of classic Australian film The Castle.
In it, an expansion of the industrial area around Melbourne's airport threatens to evict the Kerrigan family and their neighbours.
They fight the proposal and argue about the value of a home all the way to the High Court … and win.
If you haven't seen it, it's both an Australian classic and a cautionary tale for large industrial developers trying to work in suburban areas.

We have scant information, but it appears a neighbourhood dispute about power poles has influenced the trading halt of an ASX 100 company.
Data centre giant NEXTDC is valued at close to $7 billion.
Late yesterday it asked the stock exchange to suspend trading in its shares.

results.title: Samsung could double the phones in the Galaxy Z series: 'Galaxy Z Slide' rumored
results.author: nickodiaz@sbcglobal.net (Nickolas Diaz) , Nickolas Diaz
results.content:
What you need to know
- A rumor on social media suggests Samsung's foldable lineup could double in size with six phones in 2027.
- The company is allegedly preparing a TriFold 2, a Galaxy Z Fold 9 Pro, and a "Galaxy Z Slide."
- At CES 2025, Samsung Display showed off two slidable phone concepts: the "Slidable Flex Duet" and "Slidable Flex Solo."
Samsung's latest wave of foldables was incredibly popular. Okay, the Fold 8 took everything by storm, but that might not stop the company from doubling up on its offerings next year.
A rumor on X from tipster TheGalox claims Samsung is preparing for its "biggest foldable lineup ever" in 2027 (via 9to5Google). To start things off, TheGalox claims the Galaxy Z TriFold 2 could start Samsung's huge foldable stampede in 2027. This would succeed the original Z TriFold, which Samsung stopped producing after three months. Elsewhere, the tipster claims the foldables we typically expect could expand.
Currently, Samsung offers three foldables: the Galaxy Z Fold 8, Fold 8 Ultra, and Flip 8. The Fold 8 is its short, wider addition, and the Fold 8 Ultra is its standard book-style foldable. However, the tipster suggests Samsung could slip in a "Galaxy Z Fold 9 Pro." It's unclear what this would be. What's more, we're unsure about how Samsung would position this device between the Fold 9 and Fold 9 Ultra.
While we also expect to see a Flip 9, rumors say Samsung could introduce a new type of foldable: the "Galaxy Z Slide." It's almost a shame that the most interesting-sounding device is shrouded in the largest shadow, but that's only half true. If we want to at least fathom where we might go, we'll have to look back to CES 2025.
Sliding into 2027?
The Fold 8 was popular was an understandable reason. It's slightly smaller (shorter), and it felt nice to use for consumers. However, I'm curious about public reception for the Slide, if it's even happening. As a concept, the device seems really interesting. But concepts don't always transfer well into reality. These phones have to be practical, not just cool. Also, what would its price be? We all know how prices are skyrocketing.
Samsung Display was at CES 2025, if you remember our coverage about it (if you don't, here it is). As usual, the company, like other companies, showed off several prototypes. On display were the "Slidable Flex Duet" and "Solo." The Slidable Flex Duet (YouTube) would let users pull (or slide) its display out from the left and right. The device would sit at 8 inches when compact, but sliding out its display would bring it to 12.4 inches—very tablet-like.
Alternatively, you have the Solo, which would go from 13 inches to 17.3 inches. Whether or not Samsung develops one of these concepts remains to be seen. This only serves as a base to get our minds thinking.
Rumors about a TriFold sequel got underway quickly after Apple's iPhone Duo launch. Allegedly, this phone could debut in 2027 with a thinner, lighter, and more durable design. However, its price tag might remain pretty hefty at $2,800.

results.title: Judge orders fired OpenAI engineer to stay detained pre-trial over concerns about fleeing to Saudi Arabia
results.author: Stephen Council
results.content:
A former OpenAI engineer accused of bugging the AI startup's office was denied release by a San Francisco judge on Monday, meaning he'll have to mount his defense from jail.
The Justice Department arrested Abdulrahman Alfozan on October 9 and charged him with using or attempting to use a device to intercept oral communications. He's accused of placing a recording device behind a television in an OpenAI conference room — an FBI affidavit includes photos of the device wrapped in toilet paper, and a man they say is Alfozan peering behind the TV.
On Monday, the engineer wore a yellow surgical mask and a jail-issued orange sweatshirt to the San Francisco courthouse. Magistrate Judge Alex G. Tse prodded Alfozan's legal team about the risk that he might not appear for a future court hearing.
Tse said that Alfozan's wife and son had traveled to Saudi Arabia with no plans to return, and went back and forth with Yasin about a one-way ticket that Alfozan had previously booked to the country. Tse said that Saudi Arabia and the US do not have an extradition agreement, and expressed skepticism that he had sufficient ties to the Bay Area to prevent his departure.
William Pernik, Alfozan's attorney, argued that, rather than being detained, Alfozan should be fitted with an ankle monitor, ordered to stay home, and have limits placed on his use of technology. The lawyer also said Alfozan is willing to put up "essentially all the money his family has" as bond, including a roughly $1 million investment account.
"Everything this man has, he's willing to surrender, and say, 'I'm not going anywhere,'" Pernik said.
Pernik and Nas Yasin, another of Alfozan's attorneys, cited his coming naturalization interview as evidence of his local ties.
"He was weeks away from achieving every immigrant's dream in this country," Pernik said.
Yasin told Tse that she learned Alfozan's wife had obtained a short-term visitor visa to return to the US, to help improve her husband's case for ties to the Bay Area.
Tse also asked Alfozan's legal team a slew of questions about his relationship with Saudi Arabia, including a commitment by the Saudi consulate to pay his bond and support his legal effort.
Nick Parker, an assistant US attorney, appeared for the prosecution. He argued that the threat of forfeiting a $1 million bond wouldn't be enough to convince Alfozan to return if he made it out of the US, because he might be able to earn more money in Saudi Arabia.
"There is a real threat here that once he leaves, the case is over," Tse responded.
The judge scheduled the case's next hearing for early November.
OpenAI called the recording device "sophisticated" when the arrest went public, though it said it hadn't found signs that he'd taken AI model weights, source code, or customer information. OpenAI fired Alfozan.
Alfozan's charge carries a maximum penalty of 5 years. Pernik said in a statement last week that the allegations "appear wholly out of character for him."
Alfozan, 35, has a green card that makes him a lawful permanent resident of the United States. He attended MIT, then worked at Facebook (now Meta) from 2017 to 2023. After a stint at the engineering startup Nash Technologies, Alfozan joined OpenAI in 2025.
FBI agents have already taken Alfozan's Saudi passport.

results.title: Voice Of Goku Responds To AI Stealing Her Voice: ‘I can’t Forgive Them…It Makes Me Really Angry, It’s No Different Than Theft’
results.author: Alicia Haddick
results.content:
With generative AI becoming more and more of an issue for creatives in all industries, voice actors in Japan are finding their own way to fight back against the unauthorized use of their voices. Last week, the union representing Japanese voice actors issued its own guidelines regarding the use of AI, as a number of actors spoke about the personal and professional challenges they’ve faced due to the technology.
Voice actors in Japan have been taking a stand against the unauthorized use of their voice for a number of years. In 2024, a group of voice actors came together to create their own organization protesting AI voice misuse, specifically citing the lack of legal copyright protections. One voice actor, Kenjiro Tsuda, known for voice roles in Attack on Titan, Chainsaw Man, and Yu-Gi-Oh!, even sued TikTok regarding the proliferation of videos using his voice on social media, though the case was dismissed once the videos were removed. While some voice actors have advocated for systems allowing for private, licensed use of AI to replicate performers’ voices, the general view of the technology among voice actors in Japan is that it could steal their work and future opportunities.
At a press conference on Thursday, the Japan Actors Union (JAU) presented the first version of its new guidelines regarding the use of generative AI. The guidelines define these new rules as covering any audio recordings made with AI technology replicating actors’ voices, including unauthorized use for voice synthesis, deep learning, machine learning, and so forth.
As reported by Automaton, the guidelines call for anyone seeking to replicate the voice of an actor to obtain consent at every step of the process. Should an AI company wish to use an actor’s voice in AI training, it must obtain permission from the performer. Also, the authorized use of AI-generated voice is categorized as a type of “performance,” and companies will be required to pay salaries and/or royalties to actors.
At the conference were a number of voice actors who spoke against the use of the technology for unauthorized purposes. Masako Nozawa, best known for voicing Goku in the Dragon Ball franchise, told Japanese news broadcaster NHK, “I can’t forgive them for using it without my permission. It makes me really angry, it’s no different than theft. My voice is mine, as are my performances, and if that’s going to be used, even a little bit, they should ask for permission.” The voice actor also claimed that an AI version of her voice that she’d heard “lacked heart.”
The union represents roughly 2600 voice actors and actors, and the guidelines are among the first to be released in Japan regarding the use of AI for voice recordings. It sends a strong signal against AI in a country where its use is generally more accepted than it is in the U.S. And given the relative strength of Japan’s unions compared to those seen in the U.S., it’s likely this guidance will have an impact on the unauthorized use of the technology to replicate actors’ voices. Japan’s government is currently facing questions on how to deal with generative AI in response to both cyberattacks and copyright infringement, making this announcement from the JAU a notable one as the country grapples with how to address AI technology.

results.title: Russia's next tool to fight VPNs appears to be AI — and the numbers suggest it's scarily effective
results.author: Rene Millman
results.content:
Russian authorities have reportedly explored using artificial intelligence to identify and block virtual private networks with a staggering 95% effectiveness.
According to a report by Russian newspaper Kommersant, the proposal surfaced in a draft national plan for implementing AI technologies through 2030. The ambitious scheme envisioned AI models analyzing the characteristics of 70% of VPN services targeted for censorship.
While Russia’s Digital Development Ministry claims this AI measure is absent from the plan's current iteration, the underlying intent remains clear. Moscow is already heavily investing in a permanent censorship infrastructure, with recent reports highlighting plans for Russia to double its internet censorship budget.
For citizens or visitors trying to secure their connection, finding the best VPN is increasingly difficult as the state tightens its grip on circumvention tools. Currently, Russia relies on "intelligent algorithms" rather than true AI to analyze internet traffic. However, the government still intends to increase the capacity of its traffic-filtering infrastructure 2.5-fold to 954 terabits per second by 2030.
Collateral damage and false positives
An AI-powered system would sit atop Russia's existing technical systems for countering threats (TSPU), the dedicated filtering hardware already installed on telecom operators' networks.
Speaking to Kommersant, a source in the Russian networking industry explained the technical mechanics. “AI automates and accelerates the analysis of connection patterns,” the source noted. The technology would evaluate data points like packet size and timing, session duration, traffic ratios, and neighboring IP addresses to indirectly root out VPN infrastructure.
However, deploying artificial intelligence to blindly hunt down hidden traffic comes with a steep cost.
Industry sources cautioned that an AI layer could lead to a surge in false positives, trapping legitimate business and corporate traffic in the dragnet. One source estimated that the algorithmic error rate is already 5% to 6%, and early-stage AI models would likely produce a significant number of incorrect blocks.
As noted by United24 Media, rolling out such a system requires immense resources. A fully operational AI detection net requires large-scale telemetry storage, massive computing clusters for model training, and a complex infrastructure to distribute updated models directly to filtering nodes.
A broader push for "sovereign" tech
The drive to automate VPN detection is just one piece of a broader effort by Moscow to tightly control mobile communications and escalate VPN blocks. Alongside restricting circumvention tools, Russia is attempting to force the tech industry to adopt strictly domestic security standards.
A recent draft order from the Digital Development Ministry mandates that smartphones operating on Russia's future 5G networks must support "Kuznyechik", an encryption algorithm developed with participation from the FSB’s information-security centre and InfoTeKS. Scheduled to take effect on March 1, 2032, this is not part of the standard 3GPP encryption suite.
Because the algorithm must be baked into modem chipsets, it could effectively force global manufacturers like Apple and Samsung to build Russia-specific hardware just to operate in the country.
Ultimately, it appears the Kremlin is prepared to use every technological weapon at its disposal to isolate its digital borders.

results.title: France is rioting over surging inflation, skyrocketing national debt and crumbling schools. America is its sleeping twin
results.author: Nick Lichtenberg
results.content:
The fire that badly damaged Limoges’ 19th-century city hall was set on purpose, the local prefect said. By Sunday it was under control, and France was counting the damage: more than 2,400 arrests on Saturday alone, according to authorities, nearly 1,000 police and gendarmes injured, and hundreds of businesses looted in Paris, Marseille, Lyon, and other cities. Looting and fires continued Sunday night, and Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu ordered localized curfews Monday. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez admitted police “lost control” and offered to resign. President Emmanuel Macron refused.
America has worse inflation, as Fortune’s Jason Ma reported Monday. U.S. consumer prices rose 3.7% in the year through September, compared with France’s 3.4% on the EU-harmonized measure. What offsets it is growth. U.S. GDP rose 2.2% in the second quarter; unemployment is 4.2%; and wages are growing about 3.0% a year, below inflation. Meanwhile, France expects its economy to grow just 0.5% this year, and youth unemployment there is about 20%.
Set aside growth, and the two countries have a lot in common. And Americans aren’t thrilled about where the growth is coming from. Tech investment accounts for about a third of U.S. GDP growth, according to ING. Yet 39% of Americans now say AI does more harm than good, up from 31% a year ago, and 79% expect AI to cut U.S. jobs over the next decade, according to a Bentley-Gallup survey conducted in May. Among adults under 30, the harm figure is 47%. A Pew survey in June found 52% of Americans more concerned than excited about AI.
The same trap
Start with the debt. French public debt sits at a record 119% of GDP, while U.S. debt held by the public reached 100.2% of GDP at the end of March. Lecornu’s budget, which would cut France’s deficit to 5% of GDP from 5.4%, faces its first critical vote in the National Assembly on Tuesday. Washington ran a $1.992 trillion deficit in fiscal 2026, about 6.2% of GDP based on CBO’s projections. Needless to say, that’s wider than the 5.4% deficit France is rioting over.
Bond traders are treating the two countries alike. Bank of America economists Claudio Irigoyen and Antonio Gabriel recently found that the French and U.S. 10-year yields have been moving on nearly the same track, and they say the cause is the same. “When interest rates are low, governments have incentives to run bigger deficits financed with cheap debt,” they wrote in a BofA Global Research report. “However, if that ‘cheap’ debt goes to finance a structural increase of the fiscal deficit, when interest rates increase it is politically difficult to implement the necessary fiscal consolidation to put the house in order.”
The riots are what “politically difficult” looks like. In the U.S., the warning has come through the bond market. On Sept. 8, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told an audience at Southern Methodist University, “I am the house now.” The bond market disagreed. Over the next three weeks, the 30-year Treasury yield climbed as high as 5.69%, levels not seen since 2002, Johns Hopkins economist Steve Hanke and former Comptroller General David Walker wrote in Fortune.
Where the anger started
France’s protests began in classrooms. In mid-September, high school students in the Paris suburbs walked out over missing teachers, overcrowded rooms, and buildings that can’t handle the heat. They blamed years of underinvestment. Teachers and unions joined, then people angry about fuel prices and the cost of living.
American schools show the same strain, and on some measures, it’s worse. Lost class time: In France, 9.8% of teaching hours in public middle and high schools went undelivered in 2024–25, mostly because absent teachers weren’t replaced, according to the Education Ministry’s statistics office. In the U.S., the GAO found that 19% of school districts canceled classes that year because of building problems, costing about 2 million students roughly 3.5 million days of learning.
Nearly half of districts had chronic facility problems that disrupted learning. Staffing: At the start of this school year, 53% of French middle and high schools were missing at least one teacher, according to a survey of 1,033 schools by SNES-FSU, France’s largest secondary teachers union. At the start of 2024–25, 74% of U.S. public schools had trouble filling at least one vacancy with a fully certified teacher, according to the National Center for Education Statistics. Qualifications: 11.1% of French secondary teachers aren’t fully qualified, according to the OECD. In the U.S., the Learning Policy Institute estimates 387,843 teachers aren’t fully certified for their assignments and calls that an undercount.
President Trump sees another cause. “What’s happening in France is nothing less than out-of-control mass migration,” he posted on Truth Social on Oct. 6, adding that it “isn’t about schools, this is about Islam wanting to take over a once great country,” without addressing his own country’s fiscal similarities. Student demands have not mentioned immigration or religion. UBS Global Wealth Management chief economist Paul Donovan called the weekend’s violence “a different form of scapegoat economics” in a note to clients Monday.
The cushion holds as long as growth does. Market veteran Ed Yardeni argued last month that the U.S. economy is “less rate sensitive than it has ever been,” supported by wealthy retirees, large deficits, and “an extraordinary AI investment boom.”
Hanke and Walker end their column with a quote from the late MIT economist Rüdiger Dornbusch: “Crises take longer to arrive than you can possibly imagine, but when they do come, they happen faster than you can possibly imagine.”

results.summary:
France faces widespread civil unrest and property damage as the government struggles with fiscal deficits, mirroring economic and educational challenges currently impacting the United States' own stability.

### Key Points
- French authorities reported over 2,400 arrests and significant infrastructure damage, including a fire at the Limoges city hall, following nationwide protests.
- France’s public debt has reached a record 119% of GDP, while the U.S. deficit for fiscal 2026 is projected at 6.2% of GDP.
- Both nations are experiencing severe educational strain, with 74% of U.S. public schools and 53% of French secondary schools reporting teacher staffing shortages.
- Bond markets are reacting similarly to both countries, with 10-year yields tracking closely as investors weigh the risks of high government spending and rising interest rates.
- U.S. economic growth remains higher than France's 0.5% projection, though Americans express growing skepticism regarding the long-term societal impact of AI investments.

### Why it Matters
The parallel fiscal and social pressures in France and the U.S. highlight the global difficulty of implementing austerity measures when public services are failing. As both nations grapple with high debt and civil dissatisfaction, the bond market serves as a critical indicator of potential instability that could trigger rapid economic crises.
