results.title: Who Owns the Truth About Your Customer-Facing Automation Claims?
results.author: pr@cmswire.com (Ricardo Saltz Gulko)
results.content:
The Gist
- Disclosure gap. AI risk mentions in annual filings jumped from 4% of companies in 2020 to 43% in 2024, but most lack a plan to address those risks.
- Metric backfired. Presto Automation's reported non-intervention rate left out offshore human agents, and the SEC treated the figure as misleading.
- CX owns proof. Customer experience leaders are best placed to define, measure and defend what customer-facing AI actually does.
I have spent more than 20 years inside enterprise technology and global services — Oracle, Samsung, Ericsson, E2open, and a long list of high technology industrial clients since — and I have read a great deal of corporate reporting in that time. There is a pattern in how companies write about AI that I cannot stop noticing, and I think it explains more about the state of customer experience than most of the research published this year.
When a chief executive describes what AI does for the company, the language is numerical. Percentages. When he really understands what it does. Cycle times. Headcount effects. Deployment coverage. Those sentences carry decimal places because somebody had to defend them to an auditor.
When the same executive describes what AI does for customers, the register changes completely. Better. Smoother. More personalized. Enhanced. Grammatically similar, and empty.
I want to be fair before I go further. A minority of companies do measure customer outcomes properly, and I have worked with some of them. The research below shows how small that group is. My argument is about the dominant pattern and what it has started to cost.
Because the cost has changed. Securities regulators now treat unsubstantiated AI claims as an enforcement matter, and the first action against a public company concerned a system sitting directly in front of customers. There is a harder lesson inside that case, and it is one I did not expect when I started looking: replacing vague language with a confident-sounding number is not automatically an improvement. Done badly, it is a bigger exposure than the adjective was.
How Researchers Measured Vague AI Risk Disclosures in SEC Filings
I dislike arguments built on impressions, so let me use the counting that has been done.
Researchers led by Lucas Uberti-Bona Marin at Maastricht University analyzed more than 30,000 annual filings. As summarised by The Regulatory Review at the University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School, the share of companies mentioning AI risk in mandatory disclosures rose from 4% in 2020 to 43% in 2024. Acknowledgement grew more than tenfold in four years.
Then comes the part I find damning. Most of those disclosures contain no detailed plan for addressing the risks they name. The word arrived. The substance did not follow it.
Benefits Disclosed, Outage Risks Omitted
A separate team led by Ilan Strauss examined over 7,800 filings and found roughly two-thirds of AI disclosures emphasise benefits while omitting significant risks — naming systematic failures and service outages among what goes unmentioned.
Stay with that omission, because for me it is the whole article in two words. Service outages. The moment the AI stops working in front of a customer. Two-thirds of companies describing AI to investors do not mention that this can happen.
So this is not my impression. It has been counted twice, across more than 37,000 documents.
Related Article: Dear CMOs: Your Problem Isn't Your AI. It's Your Operating Model
How Often Do Companies Disclose AI Risk Without a Plan to Address It?
Mentions of AI risk in annual filings rose from 4% of companies in 2020 to 43% in 2024 across more than 30,000 filings, yet most of those disclosures lack a detailed plan for addressing the risks. A separate review of more than 7,800 filings found roughly two-thirds stress AI benefits while omitting risks such as systematic failures and service outages.
Why Companies Choose Vague Language for Customer-Facing AI
Nobody drafts a filing carelessly. I have sat on the corporate side of these documents and they pass through counsel, committees and personal liability before anyone signs. Every omission is a choice.
So ask what the pattern optimizes for. Specific claims about internal gains are safe: true, verifiable, flattering. Specific claims about customer outcomes are dangerous in both directions. A bad number discloses a problem. A good number creates an expectation you must then sustain every quarter.
Vagueness is the rational choice. Saying AI improved the customer experience commits you to nothing, cannot be falsified, and cannot be compared with next year's version of the same sentence.
Rational, and no longer safe.
Why Do Companies Keep Customer-Facing AI Claims Vague in Filings?
Specific claims about internal gains are verifiable and flattering, while specific customer-outcome numbers either disclose a problem or set an expectation the company must sustain every quarter. Vague language commits to nothing and cannot be falsified, which made it the rational choice until regulators began treating unsubstantiated AI claims as an enforcement matter.
How Presto Automation's Customer-Facing AI Metric Drew SEC Action
In January 2025 the Securities and Exchange Commission brought what is widely regarded as its first AI-washing enforcement action against a public reporting company. I want to underline what the product was, because most commentary skipped past it. This was not a trading algorithm. It was a customer service system.
Presto Automation, listed on Nasdaq until September 2024, sold a voice product automating drive-through ordering at quick-service restaurants. As Ropes & Gray sets out, the company described that product in Forms 8-K, S-4 and other registration statements filed between 2021 and 2023 as if it were internally built and claimed it eliminated human order taking. The Commission found the underlying technology was owned and operated by a third party, and that the company relied heavily on human employees in other countries to complete those orders.
Offshore Agents Behind the Non-Intervention Rate
Then the detail that changed how I think about this whole subject, because it is the opposite of vagueness.
Lowenstein Sandler's account of the findings records that the company used terms such as automated order completion and non-intervention rates in investor presentations, while running human agents in offshore locations including the Philippines and India. It eventually acknowledged that more than 70% of orders through its in-house version required human intervention, that certain locations required intervention on every single order, and that the average non-intervention rate was 85%.
Read what happened there. This company did not hide behind adjectives. It published a precise, confident, customer-facing metric — a non-intervention rate — and the precision itself became the problem, because the number described something other than what investors reasonably understood it to mean.
Why a Metric Without a Definition Is Riskier Than an Adjective
I have been arguing for years that our profession needs harder numbers. This case forced me to sharpen that position. A decimal point is not evidence. A metric without a defensible definition and a control behind it is more dangerous than an adjective, because people act on it — investors, boards and eventually customers who were promised something the system does not do.
Cooley notes that the Commission imposed a cease-and-desist order without a civil money penalty, given the company's financial condition and remedial steps. The reputational and structural findings did the damage instead.
How Did Presto Automation's Non-Intervention Rate Mislead Investors?
Presto reported high non-intervention rates for its drive-thru voice ordering product, but the figure counted only orders completed without restaurant staff stepping in, while offshore human agents in the Philippines and India handled most orders. The SEC settled with a cease-and-desist order and no civil money penalty.
Why Missing Disclosure Controls Turned Presto's AI Claims Into a Violation
It would be convenient to treat this as one badly behaved company. I do not read it that way.
As DLA Piper records, the alleged violations covered Section 17(a)(2) of the Securities Act and Section 13(a) of the Exchange Act with related rules, and the order also found the company had failed to establish and maintain disclosure controls and procedures. There was no reliable process for deciding what got said about the product.
In my view that is a customer experience failure wearing a securities-law costume. Nobody owned the question of what the system actually did for the customer, so the description drifted toward what the market wanted to hear, and no control existed to pull it back. I have seen that drift inside large organizations many times. It rarely starts with dishonesty. It starts with an unowned question.
A $42 Million Shopping App Case Raises the Same Question
The wider pattern matters too. Holland & Knight's review of 2025 places this case alongside a separate matter in which the Commission alleged more than $42 million was raised on claims that a shopping application used AI to complete purchases when, according to the Commission, nearly all orders were processed manually. Both turn on one question: how much of this is actually the machine?
That question belongs to whoever owns the customer journey. In most organizations I work with, nobody has been asked it.
What Disclosure Control Failure Did the SEC Find at Presto Automation?
The SEC found Presto failed to establish and maintain disclosure controls and procedures, leaving no reliable process for deciding what the company said about its customer-facing product. A separate SEC complaint over a shopping app alleged more than $42 million was raised on claims of AI-completed purchases that humans processed manually.
What Regulators Now Expect From Customer-Facing AI Claims
Norton Rose Fulbright's guidance is that regulators have not invented new theories for AI. They are applying long-standing standards of accuracy, transparency and internal control to a new context. Vague investor-facing claims — describing a product simply as AI-powered — signal a need to understand what the tools, models and data actually do and how they differ from ordinary rule-based processing. Their conclusion is that whoever handles public communications must know the right questions to ask about the technology.
I read that as a job description, and I think it is ours. Somebody has to state precisely what the AI does to a customer, how well, and on what evidence. No other function can.
A Three-Step Order for Proving What Customer-Facing AI Delivers
The following table highlights the most important lessons, actions and strategic considerations emerging from the three steps for substantiating customer-facing AI claims, listed in the order they should happen.
| Key Area | What Happened | Why It Matters | Recommended Action | 
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Audit your own adjectives | Claims about what AI does for customers run through investor communications, press releases and product marketing without evidence behind them. | Anything without an answer is a credibility problem and, increasingly, a legal one. | Take four quarters of those materials and highlight every claim about what AI does for customers. For each one, ask what evidence you would produce if a regulator, a journalist or your largest account asked you to substantiate it. | 
| 2. Describe the loop honestly, then measure the handover | In the enforcement order, the human intervention rate was the entire story, and it was the number nobody described accurately. | Hybrid service is entirely defensible. Misdescribing it is not. The handover is also where deployments actually fail, which I argued in AI in CX Is Not the Problem: Escalation Failures Are the Real Trust Gap. | Write down, for each customer-facing system, what is fully automated, what is decision-support with a human deciding, and what stays human. | 
| 3. Build one substantiated customer number and freeze its definition | Dashboards fill up with decorative figures that don't show a customer outcome moved. | One defensible number beats twenty decorative ones, and it is the only kind that survives being challenged. | Pick one figure showing a customer outcome moved, such as repeat contacts avoided, renewal for AI-touched customers against a matched group, or resolution verified rather than assumed. Write the method down before collection starts. | 
How Can CX Leaders Substantiate Claims About Customer-Facing AI?
Audit four quarters of investor communications, press releases and product marketing for unsupported claims about what AI does for customers, then document which parts of each customer-facing system are automated, human-assisted or fully human. Build one customer outcome metric, such as repeat contacts avoided, with its method written down before data collection starts.
Why SEC Scrutiny Gives CX Leaders an Opening
Most people in my field will read this as compliance arriving on top of everything else. I think that reading is wrong and strategically expensive.
Look at the position we are in. Regulators, investors and increasingly large B2B customers are converging on a demand for specificity about what AI does at the point of contact. The function best placed to supply it — the only one that can say what happened to the customer, with evidence — has spent a decade struggling to get its numbers taken seriously in a boardroom.
The requirement has changed sides. Precision about customer-facing AI is no longer something we have to lobby for. It is something the organisation will need from somebody, fairly soon.
Who Writes the Description of Customer-Facing AI
So the real question is not whether your company will eventually describe its customer-facing AI in verifiable terms. It is whether that description gets written by people who understand customers, or by people who understand liability. Those two documents look very different, and only one of them improves anything.
Start with the adjectives. Every one of them is a measurement somebody decided not to take — and, as that company discovered, replacing them with a number you cannot defend is worse than leaving them where they were.
Learn how you can join our contributor community.
results.summary:
Public companies are increasingly citing AI risks in annual filings, yet many lack concrete plans to address these disclosures, drawing heightened scrutiny from the Securities and Exchange Commission.

### Key Points
- AI risk mentions in annual corporate filings surged from 4% in 2020 to 43% in 2024, according to research from Maastricht University.
- A review of over 7,800 filings revealed that two-thirds of companies highlight AI benefits while omitting critical risks like service outages.
- The SEC initiated its first AI-washing enforcement action against Presto Automation for misleading investors about its drive-thru voice ordering technology.
- Presto Automation claimed high "non-intervention" rates while relying on offshore human agents in India and the Philippines to complete the majority of orders.
- Regulators are now applying established standards of accuracy and internal control to AI, penalizing companies that fail to substantiate customer-facing claims.

### Why it Matters
The shift toward regulatory enforcement means that vague or unsubstantiated claims about AI performance now pose significant legal and reputational risks to public companies. By establishing clear, defensible metrics for customer-facing AI, organizations can move beyond empty marketing language and satisfy the growing demand for transparency from investors and regulators alike.

results.title: Clevetura S Keyboard Review: Swipe Across the Keys Instead of Reaching for a Mouse
results.author: JC Torres
results.content:
PROS:
- Innovative combination of keyboard and touchpad in one
- Compact, lightweight design
- Customizable gestures and sensitivity
- Supports 3 Bluetooth and 1 USB-C connections
CONS:
- Has a bit of a learning curve for accuracy and speed
- Premium price tag
Keyboards and mice have shared our desks for decades, but our hands still have to travel between them whenever typing gives way to clicking. That familiar shuffle becomes especially noticeable when there’s barely enough room for a laptop, let alone another accessory. The Clevetura S offers an interesting solution by turning the keys themselves into a touchpad, giving your fingers another way to get around without leaving the keyboard.
Also known as the CLVX S, this compact, 78-key keyboard brings Clevetura’s TouchOnKeys technology to a more portable design. The Windows version reviewed here can handle familiar gestures without additional software, although there’s plenty to customize if you want to. More importantly, it makes an unusual interaction surprisingly useful, even if sliding across letters and keeping resting fingers from triggering gestures take a little getting used to.
Designer: Clevetura
Aesthetics
Upfront, the Clevetura S looks almost like someone forgot to leave space between the keys. The flat keycaps sit unusually close together, giving the 78-key layout a tidy, almost tiled appearance. There’s a practical reason for that, of course. Fingers need to travel across the surface as comfortably as they press down on it, and generous gaps would make that second job considerably less inviting.
An anodized aluminum base gives the keyboard its silver lower half, while polycarbonate covers the top and ABS plastic forms the keycaps. Both black and white versions retain that silver body, which is particularly noticeable against the darker finish. I would have preferred an entirely black option for a simpler look, though the contrast does make the thin profile a little more obvious when viewed from the side.
Otherwise, there isn’t much to distract from that continuous field of keys, save for the extra markings explaining their secondary functions. Two buttons below the spacebar provide physical left- and right-click controls, recalling the arrangement on older laptops. Then there’s the per-key RGB lighting, which can turn this relatively understated keyboard into something considerably more colorful. Fortunately, those lights also have practical roles beyond decorating your desk.
Ergonomics
At roughly 403g, the Clevetura S doesn’t ask for much commitment when you’re packing a laptop bag. Its body measures approximately 11.5 inches wide, 5.12 inches deep, and just 0.49 inches (12.4mm) thick, making it easy to accommodate on smaller desks, too. The closely fitted keycaps don’t leave many edges sticking out, although I’d still use the included fabric pouch rather than let them rub against everything else.
The scissor switches feel familiar if you’re coming from a decent laptop keyboard, with around 1.2mm of travel. Typing is perfectly serviceable, though it probably won’t steal the attention of someone devoted to mechanical switches. Folding feet let you raise the back, but there’s only one elevated position. That keeps setup simple, provided you’re comfortable with either the flat profile or the available incline.
The more interesting benefit shows up when you need to scroll through a reference or reposition the cursor between sentences. Instead of reaching sideways, you can make that movement right where you’ve been typing. Your chair and screen position still matter, of course. The Clevetura S simply reduces the back-and-forth, although its flat, closely fitted keys take some getting used to when finding your usual typing rhythm.
Performance
The central key area doubles as the touchpad, automatically switching between recognizing finger movements and registering keypresses. Sliding across letters feels a little peculiar at first, but my fingers didn’t catch on the edges, and pointer control worked well. Scrolling through a document becomes especially convenient when you’re jumping back into writing every few moments. A light tap handles clicking without requiring you to press a letter.
That automatic switching does have to contend with personal habits, however. Mine involves keeping fingers on the home row, which happens to sit inside the touchpad area. This frequently triggered three-finger gestures when I hadn’t intended anything of the sort. Sensitivity adjustments and the option to disable unwanted gestures provide useful flexibility, though finding the right balance is something to budget time for rather than expect immediately.
Clevetura’s Adaptive Intelligence, or AI, can help by selecting a sensitivity level after studying 10,000 typed characters. Training requires the TouchOnKeys app and a USB connection, with touch recognition disabled while it runs. A separate mouse is handy during that process, although you can pause training if necessary. Thankfully, this particular AI has a fairly modest assignment: learning when your fingers mean to type rather than swipe.
The lighting makes that second role easier to follow, and a little more entertaining, too. In my setup, a white trail followed my finger across the keys, almost like leaving a trace of magic behind. Checking the battery dims the surrounding lighting and uses illuminated number keys to show the remaining charge. Even the function row gets involved, with touch sliders for volume and backlight brightness.
Windows recognizes supported touchpad gestures without installing additional software, but TouchOnKeys opens up more settings, including profiles for different apps. Three Bluetooth slots and a USB-C connection let you select between up to four devices, one at a time. That’s useful if your desk serves more than one computer. The cable also handles charging and provides the wired connection required for firmware updates.
Clevetura advertises up to 44 hours of continuous use without backlighting, which is an important qualification for anyone drawn to those colorful effects. That’s the manufacturer’s estimate rather than a result measured here, so it shouldn’t become a promise of weeks between charges. Wired operation remains available at a desk, while wireless endurance deserves particular attention if you’re planning to travel with the lighting switched on.
Sustainability
The aluminum and plastic construction follows a fairly familiar recipe, and there’s no documented recycled content to give the CLVX S a particular advantage on materials. Clevetura rates its keys for 3 million presses, although that remains a manufacturer specification rather than a prediction of service life. The more useful question is how easily this unusual keyboard can be maintained once everyday use starts leaving its mark.
Here, the same integration that makes TouchOnKeys possible also limits what owners can replace. Clevetura warns against removing or swapping keycaps because doing so can damage the keyboard, and the battery isn’t easily user-replaceable either. Routine surface cleaning and manufacturer support therefore matter more than they would on a board designed for tinkering. It’s worth understanding that arrangement before expecting mechanical-keyboard levels of customization or straightforward repairs.
Value
At $199, discounted from $209, the Windows model sits well above the price of many conventional compact keyboards. The extra cost is easier to understand when you consider what you’re paying for: typing and pointer control in the same footprint. Separate devices offer more freedom to choose each component, but they also need more space. Clevetura’s appeal is having those everyday functions share one portable object.
That could be particularly attractive when you’re writing code, checking references, or moving between shortcuts and controls in creative software. Quick navigation stays close, even if detailed drawing or extended pointer work still calls for a separate mouse. The Clevetura S doesn’t have to handle every task equally well to be useful. Its value depends on how often you make those small trips away from the keys.
Verdict
Combining a keyboard and touchpad sounds simple enough until your fingers have to tell the two jobs apart. Clevetura gives that idea a thoughtful physical form, from the closely fitted keys to lighting that explains what’s happening beneath your hands. My habit of resting on the home row made gesture sensitivity especially important, but the pointer control itself worked well and gave the unusual surface a practical purpose.
The Clevetura CLVX S makes the strongest impression when space is limited and typing is regularly interrupted by a scroll or a click. Its price deserves consideration, and the flat surface won’t replace everyone’s favorite keyboard feel. Still, there’s something pleasing about editing a sentence, sliding across the letters to move the cursor, and carrying on without sending a hand off to find another device.
results.summary:
The Clevetura S is a compact, 78-key keyboard featuring integrated TouchOnKeys technology that allows users to control a cursor and perform gestures directly on the surface of the keys.

### Key Points
- The device features a 78-key layout with scissor switches, an anodized aluminum base, and per-key RGB lighting.
- It supports connectivity for up to four devices, including three Bluetooth channels and one USB-C wired connection.
- Users can customize gesture sensitivity and settings via the TouchOnKeys app, which includes an AI-driven training mode to distinguish typing from swiping.
- The keyboard measures 11.5 by 5.12 inches, weighs 403g, and is priced at $199.
- Battery life is rated for up to 44 hours of continuous use when backlighting is disabled.

### Why it Matters
By merging typing and navigation into a single footprint, the Clevetura S offers a space-saving solution for users working in cramped environments or on the go. While the premium price and learning curve may deter some, it provides a unique workflow efficiency for professionals who frequently switch between text entry and cursor control.

results.title: Apple Limiting U.S. iPhone Duo Orders to Two Per Customer
results.author: Juli Clover
results.content:
Apple is only allowing customers in the United States to purchase a maximum of two iPhone Duos. Attempting to purchase more than two on the website or the Apple Store app gives the following notice: "A maximum of 2 iPhone Duo can be purchased per customer. Please adjust the total quantity of iPhone Duo in your order before checking out."
Some Reddit users describe the U.S. purchase limit as new, but we couldn't confirm if it was in place when pre-orders started on October 16. The Reddit thread has reports from customers claiming to have been able to purchase four Duos and from those who say they were limited to two.
Apple had clear two-per-customer restrictions listed in countries like China, Singapore, and Hong Kong, but the U.S. website doesn't mention the limit until you try to add more than two Duos to the cart.
Launch day delivery stock sold out within minutes of pre-orders going live, and many customers received delivery dates in November or December. Apple has been moving up some delivery dates, so it may be able to fulfill demand earlier than expected for some customers who pre-ordered early.
results.summary:
Apple has implemented a two-unit purchase limit for the new iPhone Duo in the United States, restricting customers from buying more than two devices per order online.

### Key Points
- Apple’s U.S. website and app now automatically block orders exceeding two iPhone Duo units per customer.
- Similar purchase restrictions were previously confirmed for customers in China, Singapore, and Hong Kong.
- Initial launch day inventory for the iPhone Duo sold out within minutes of the October 16 pre-order launch.
- Some customers who secured early pre-orders are seeing their estimated delivery dates moved up from November or December.
- Reports from users remain inconsistent regarding whether this policy was enforced at the start of the pre-order period.

### Why it Matters
This purchase cap suggests that Apple is managing tight supply chain constraints to prevent bulk buying and ensure broader product availability for individual consumers. The move reflects ongoing efforts to stabilize inventory distribution as the company works to fulfill high demand and improve delivery timelines.

results.title: How HSBC’s Sharia fund invested millions in Israeli war-linked firms
results.author: Yashraj Sharma
results.content:
The United Kingdom’s biggest so-called Islamic law-compliant fund spent more than $130m to buy shares in several companies linked to the Israeli military amid an ongoing genocide in Gaza, pogroms in the occupied West Bank and the occupation of southern Lebanon.
HSBC, Europe’s second-largest bank, invested the funds through its Islamic Global Equity Index Fund in companies linked to Israel’s military supply chain – from components used in weapons to technology and equipment with military applications.
The firms range from US tech giant Palantir to the world’s second-largest arms company, RTX.
Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza has killed about 74,500 Palestinians since October 2023, including more than 1,500 killed since a “ceasefire” was agreed upon a year ago, devastating the enclave of 2.3 million people.
Investments by the HSBC fund raise several questions, including whether money marketed as compliant with Islamic law can flow into companies linked to the Israeli military.
What is HSBC’s Islamic Global Equity Index Fund?
With more than $8bn in assets, HSBC’s Islamic fund channels the savings of investors, expected to be predominantly Muslim, into global equities screened against Islamic financial principles.
The bank’s website for the fund says it delivers “both investment returns and better outcomes for society as a whole”, describing its Islamic fund philosophy as “ethical investments that enhance society”.
It is supposed to exclude businesses and financial practices deemed forbidden under its Islamic law screening rules, with oversight from a religion-specific committee.
HSBC says it has an independent Islamic committee consisting of two internationally renowned Muslim scholars overseeing investment in the fund “to ensure compliance with Islamic principles”.
Under its own philosophy that dictates the Islamic fund’s investments, as reviewed by Al Jazeera, HSBC says it ensures that a “company has no significant exposure to non-permissible revenue sources such as selling goods or services related to … weapons”.
Wahyu Jatmiko, a lecturer at the University of Southampton Business School, with a focus on Islamic finance, told Al Jazeera there are “strong grounds to criticise HSBC’s governance, transparency, and handling of investors’ ethical expectations”.
“The strongest concern is the apparent tension between its stated restrictions and the reported investments,” he said.
“This should also be a lesson for the whole Islamic finance industry. The ‘Sharia’ label should mean something; it carries expectations about investing differently and realising the higher ethical objectives of Islamic law,” Jatmiko told Al Jazeera.
An HSBC spokesperson told Al Jazeera in a statement, “We understand how important it is that funds like this reflect the values of those who invest in them.”
“We take any concerns from our clients seriously and will review this matter carefully, in partnership with independent expert advisors, to assess whether the approach still meets investors’ expectations. We commit to conducting this review swiftly and communicating any necessary actions to our customers,” the statement added.
To which companies did HSBC channel its Sharia-compliant fund?
An analysis of the HSBC Islamic fund’s activities in the first half of 2026 shows that the bank bought shares in at least five companies linked to the Israeli military’s wars in the Middle East.
The Middle East Eye and Hyphen publications first reported these purchases.
Palantir
Palantir Technologies, a US data analytics and artificial intelligence company, has faced scrutiny over its support for Israel’s military. In January 2024, the company announced a strategic partnership with Israel’s Ministry of Defence to support “war-related missions” and held a board meeting in Tel Aviv in solidarity with the country.
Hyphen reported last week that HSBC’s fund bought $38.3m worth of shares in the US tech giant.
Palantir’s software integrates large volumes of data to help military and intelligence agencies analyse information and make operational decisions.
A United Nations report in June 2025 identified Palantir as expanding its support to the Israeli military since the start of the genocidal Gaza war. The report said there were “reasonable grounds” to believe the company provided automatic predictive policing technology used for automated decision-making in the battlefield, to process data and generate lists of targets, including through AI systems such as “Lavender”, “Gospel” and “Where’s Daddy?”.
The US military also reportedly relied on Palantir’s systems in falsely identifying a school in the Iranian city of Minab as a target in a strike that killed more than 150 people, mostly children, on February 28, the first day of the US-Israel war on Iran.
Senior figures at the UN have also argued that technologies such as Palantir’s determine the pace and scale at which the Israeli army is able to target people.
RTX
HSBC’s fund also bought $35.7m worth of shares in RTX, among the world’s biggest arms companies, in the first half of this year, the Middle East Eye reported.
RTX Corporation is a US defence company whose businesses include Raytheon, a major manufacturer of missiles, air-defence systems, and military technologies.
Through Raytheon, the corporation partners with the Israeli government-owned Rafael Advanced Defense Systems company to manufacture components and Tamir interceptor missiles for the Iron Dome air-defence system.
Raytheon and the Israeli company also jointly developed David’s Sling, another Israeli missile-defence system. Raytheon also makes Tomahawk missiles and MIM-104 Patriot missile systems for the US military, which have been used in the war on Iran, in addition to providing components to F-series jets that are deployed in the occupied Palestinian territory.
Analog Devices
HSBC invested $20.3m in shares of Analog Devices, a US semiconductor company that has shipped components to Elbit Systems, Israel’s biggest privately owned weapons manufacturer, amid Israel’s genocide in Gaza.
Analog makes electronic components used in surveillance systems, aircraft and precision-guided munitions.
In July 2025, Irish investigative outlet The Ditch reported that Analog Devices International, the company’s Irish-registered subsidiary, shipped components from its factory in the Philippines to Elbit Systems in August, October and November 2024.
Honeywell
In June 2024, Israel bombed the UN-run al-Sardi school in central Gaza’s Nuseirat refugee camp, killing nearly 40 Palestinians, including at least 14 children and nine women.
A measurement unit from the missile, used to aid with precision targeting, was manufactured by Honeywell, a US conglomerate that specialises in the design and delivery of sensors and guidance devices that are used in a variety of military weapons, as a 2024 analysis by Al Jazeera showed.
The HSBC fund bought $18.9m worth of shares in Honeywell International.
Rolls-Royce
HSBC invested $17.6m in Rolls-Royce Holdings, the only British company identified in the list so far, which manufactures engines and propulsion systems for military aircraft and armoured vehicles.
Its German subsidiary, MTU Aero Engine, has supplied power systems for Israeli military vehicles, including the Merkava tank, Namer armoured personnel carrier and Eitan armoured vehicle.
In 2023, Rolls-Royce Solutions America received a US military contract to supply power packs for Israel’s Eitan vehicles, with further funding added later. In April 2025, the US approved a potential $180m sale of additional Eitan engines.
How did HSBC’s Islamic fund greenlight weapons firms?
Islamic finance experts explained to Al Jazeera that there are multiple industry standards, at times specific to benchmarks, on what qualifies as an Islamic finance-compliant fund, especially as they are left to the interpretation of scholars.
“Scholars translate Islamic principles into practical rules within institutions shaped by regulation and commercial pressures,” Jatmiko told Al Jazeera. For example, he pointed out, there are differences between how the S&P and Dow Jones indices identify an Islamic finance-compliant company. The S&P’s standard Islamic finance indices do not directly exclude defence companies, whereas the Dow Jones Islamic Market indices exclude them under their screening methods.
Muhammed Ebrahim, a professor of finance at the Business School of Durham University, said there is a “critical gap” in the screening process that assesses the company’s declared principal activities, not the end use of its products or its customers.
“A company classified as ‘technology’ or ‘industrial’ can pass the business activity screen even if its products end up in weapons systems. This is precisely the issue in the HSBC case,” Ebrahim told Al Jazeera. “The screening does not typically trace a company’s supply chain to determine whether its components are used in civilian harm.”
However, an investment can technically be Islamic finance-compliant, but ethically incompatible with Islamic principles, and “the HSBC case illustrates this gap starkly”, he said.
“The maqasid of Islamic law [goals of Islamic doctrine] – including the preservation of life [hifz al-nafs] and justice [adl] – are not captured by a mechanical sector-exclusion test,” said Ebrahim.
He argues that screening should trigger a threshold over any involvement in weapons production or military contracting, review any indirect involvement, and trace the end-use of products.
“The current system does none of these systematically. It relies on sector classification and financial ratios, not supply-chain and end-use analysis,” he said.
HSBC has failed its Muslim customers by investing in Israeli military-linked companies, said Ebrahim.
“The fund is marketed as ‘Sharia-compliant’ to Muslim savers, many of whom hold it through halal pension schemes,” he argued, adding that “those investors reasonably expect that their money is not funding companies implicated in civilian harm”.
Ebrahim and Jatmiko agreed on a core issue: that Islamic finance outsources “ethical judgement to screening providers whose methodologies are opaque and whose definitions are narrow”.
“The HSBC case is a wake-up call: technical compliance is not the same as ethical fidelity,” said Ebrahim. “Funds that invoke the Sharia label have a responsibility to ensure that the substance, not just the form, aligns with the objectives of the law.”
results.summary:
HSBC’s Islamic Global Equity Index Fund faces scrutiny after investing over $130 million in companies linked to the Israeli military, raising concerns regarding its Sharia-compliant investment standards.

### Key Points
- The HSBC fund invested in five companies linked to the Israeli military, including Palantir, RTX, Analog Devices, Honeywell, and Rolls-Royce.
- Investments included $38.3 million in Palantir and $35.7 million in RTX, a major manufacturer of missile and air-defense components.
- The fund, which manages over $8 billion, is marketed as ethically aligned with Islamic principles and overseen by an independent committee of scholars.
- Experts note a "critical gap" in screening processes that focus on a company's primary sector rather than the end-use of its products in military supply chains.
- HSBC has pledged to review the matter with independent advisors to determine if the fund’s current approach meets investor expectations.

### Why it Matters
This controversy highlights a significant disconnect between technical financial screening and the ethical expectations of investors seeking Sharia-compliant products. It raises broader questions about the transparency of Islamic finance governance and whether current industry standards effectively prevent capital from supporting military activities and civilian harm.

results.title: Artists Behind Olivia Rodrigo ‘Expectations’ Music Video Debunk AI Accusations
results.author: Jaeden Pinder
results.content:
On Friday, Olivia Rodrigo unveiled a music video for the Chappell Roan-assisted remix of “Expectations,” though some viewers believed AI may have been involved in the video’s creative process. However, one of the art team’s designers and Rodrigo’s official fan account showed behind-the-scenes footage featuring hand-drawn 2D and 3D animations, analog treatments, and seemingly no AI involvement. (A rep for Rodrigo did not immediately respond to Rolling Stone’s request for comment.)
The AI accusations mainly sparked from a scene beginning around the three-minute mark of the video. In it, a series of retro logos and animations of Rodrigo and Roan fly through the frame. Viewers pointed to the inconsistencies on Rodrigo and Roan’s fingers as possible proof of generative-AI usage in the video.
The video posted by @LiviesHQ compiles drafts of drawings, recordings of 3D animations, and more. Jack Harrison led the analog treatment for “Expectations,” which gives the video its retro, low-fi flair. The art team used 2D and 3D software to create the animations, plugged the designs’ file into a Windows Vista PC, and then filmed the animations on the Vista’s screen through a hi-res camera.
The “Expectations” video finds Rodrigo and Roan parodying a series of retro game shows, including The Price Is Right, Jeopardy!, and Wheel of Fortune. It also features a wealth of cameos: David Byrne appears as a game-show host, while drag queen Aquaria and punk duo the Venus Twins appear in a Family Feud spoof called “Sister Squabble.”
Earlier this month, Rodrigo revealed she would “never” use AI in her music in a cover story for The Hollywood Reporter. “Absolutely no. Hard line on that,” she said. “The closest I’d ever got is that once, me and [producer] Dan [Nigro] were like, ‘God, I wonder what ideas ChatGPT would have for an Olivia Rodrigo title,’ and they’re all fucking awful.”
results.summary:
Olivia Rodrigo and Chappell Roan’s new music video for the “Expectations” remix faced online accusations of AI usage, which the production team refuted with behind-the-scenes evidence of manual animation.

### Key Points
- Fans speculated that generative AI created inconsistent finger details in a scene featuring retro logos and animations.
- Designer Jack Harrison utilized analog treatments, 2D software, and 3D modeling to achieve the video's low-fi aesthetic.
- Production footage shows the team filming digital animations off a Windows Vista monitor to create the final retro effect.
- The video parodies classic game shows like The Price Is Right and Jeopardy! with cameos from David Byrne and Aquaria.
- Rodrigo previously stated in a Hollywood Reporter interview that she maintains a strict policy against using AI in her creative work.

### Why it Matters
This controversy highlights the growing public sensitivity toward AI-generated content in professional media and the resulting scrutiny of artistic production methods. By providing transparent behind-the-scenes documentation, the production team successfully countered misinformation and reinforced the artist's commitment to human-led creative processes.

results.title: Elon Musk Vows To Give a SpaceX Share To 'Every Kid In America'
results.author: BeauHD
results.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from CNN: Elon Musk has said he will give every child in America a stake in SpaceX, his $2 trillion aerospace and artificial intelligence company, as tech firms face intensifying scrutiny over their impact on society. "Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America," he wrote on X on Monday. "This will be the first of many."
SpaceX only began trading publicly in June (and after the biggest initial public offering in history). The company's shares were trading for about $146 when the market closed on Friday. Musk's proposal was thin on detail. It is not clear how those shares would be distributed to the tens of millions of American children or whether all of them would even be eligible. According to the United States Census Bureau, there are roughly 73 million people under the age of 18, making Musk's potential giveaway worth about $10.7 billion at SpaceX's current share price. The move came in response to Anthropic's announcement on Sunday that it will commit at least 5% of its shares to a "Public Benefit Fund" that will donate money to social causes. "I recommend giving the shares directly to the public," Musk said in a reply to Anthropic's announcement. "This is what I will be doing."
results.summary:
Elon Musk announced plans to distribute SpaceX shares to every child in America, a proposal that could involve over 73 million minors and cost approximately $10.7 billion.

### Key Points
- Elon Musk pledged on X to give one SpaceX share to every American child starting next year.
- SpaceX shares closed at approximately $146 per share as of the most recent market data.
- The U.S. Census Bureau estimates there are roughly 73 million people under the age of 18 in the country.
- The announcement follows Anthropic’s commitment to donate 5% of its shares to a public benefit fund.
- Specific logistical details regarding the distribution process and eligibility criteria remain undisclosed by Musk.

### Why it Matters
This proposal highlights a growing trend of tech leaders attempting to address public concerns regarding corporate social responsibility and wealth distribution. If implemented, the move would represent a massive transfer of private equity to the public, potentially setting a new precedent for how major corporations engage with societal impact.

results.title: Most Event Viewer errors are normal, and you probably shouldn't be looking at them in the first place
results.author: João Carrasqueira
results.content:
Whenever you run into problems with Windows 11, it's usually time to start diving into all the possible causes. One of the ways to do that, and one we've recommended quite often here at XDA, is to use Event Viewer to find possible errors that led to a crash or blue screen.
But digging through Event Viewer can be a scary experience. Not because it's confusing or complicated necessarily, but because it will show you a lot of errors that will make you think something is wrong, even if your PC is functioning exactly as expected.
Event Viewer errors have tiers
They're not all the same
When you open Event Viewer, you'll see a long list of messages with a few different types, mostly falling under Information, Warning, Error, or Critical categories. Information messages are the ones you'll most likely overlook, especially as they're also the most frequent type of message and just indicate that a specific thing has happened on the system. It usually means that the task was completed successfully.
You might be tempted to pour over all the other kinds of messages, but generally, there's not much of a reason to. With warning messages, they usually just indicate that a configuration or program could cause an error at some point, or that some configuration should be changed or checked for safety. Most of the time, there's nothing you really need or want to change.
Even the error messages don't necessarily have to mean anything big. Event Viewer logs pretty much everything that's happening on your computer — every attempt to connect to a service or the internet, or to load a file or program. A lot of the time, these things can fil on a first attempt for any number of reasons, and then function exactly as expected on a subsequent attempt, all without it ever being brought up to you during normal use.
As of writing this, my laptop indicates there were 64 error messages and 108 warning messages in the last 24 hours, yet I've had no issues whatsoever. Of course, that's not to say Error messages are never important, but unless you're seeing an actual problem that ties into it. Failures and retries are natural parts of how your PC operates, and unless you know something is getting in the way of your work, there's no reason to lose sleep to peer through every error message in Event Viewer.
Critical errors are (usually) more important
You'll know when these happen
The one kind of message you probably shouldn't ignore when looking at Event Viewer is whatever falls under the Critical category, and the name is fairly self-explanatory. These errors indicate that the system encountered an error so severe that it caused a program or service to crash or close.
Many times, you'll see this error because your entire system crashed due to a Windows component failing, resulting in a blue screen of death. Whenever you see one of these screens, you can actually see an error message that tells you what to look for in Event Viewer, and that's where you can find more information about what actually caused it so you can find potential solutions.
Still, critical errors are also not always indicative of larger problems with your PC. Sometimes, your computer may simply shut down unexpectedly for reasons unrelated to the OS, and that would be marked as a Critical error because something caused the computer to shut down, but it wouldn't have to mean anything is wrong with the system. You can even cause one yourself by using a command such as taskkill /IM svchost.exe /f in your terminal (this will shut down your computer, so save your work beforehand).
It's a troubleshooting tool, not a maintenance system
Use it when you need it
The best way to look at it is that Event Viewer is more of a troubleshooting tool than a way to monitor your system regularly. You should look at the logs in Event Viewer when you're running into concrete problems. Going into Event Viewer and looking for the right timestamp and message can help you figure whether something is truly wrong with your system or not.
That could be because of a blue screen or application crash, but there are other application errors that could end up there, so it's always worth a look to see if you can spot the cause and eventually find a solution.
But if you're just doing a regular checkup to make sure everything is running as intended, there's no use in jumping the shark just because you see dozens of error messages in Event Viewer. Ultimately, it's there to help you diagnose a problem you already have, not to help you find new ones.
There may be better alternatives, too
Event Viewer makes things more stressful than they need to be
If you want to keep an eye on your PC's reliability and make sure things are running smoothly, there are other tools in Windows 11 that may do a better job of this than Event Viewer. One is Reliability Monitor, which organizes error and information messages more neatly into an overview that makes it easier to understand what's been happening on your PC. The information is essentially the same, but it's presented in a much clearer way.
Meanwhile, troubleshooting BSODs can be made easier with a program called BlueScreenView, which focuses just on the errors that caused blue screens and, again, provides a less daunting interface to look at them.
Otherwise, if you want to keep your system running smoothly, there are other places you might want to look to help improve performance or make sure you're not piling up unnecessary files and apps. Check Task Manager for unnecessary startup apps, look through your app list for anything you might not need anymore, and run malware checks somewhat regularly. I always recommend MalwareBytes as the best way to detect all kinds of malware, though there are other great options.
results.summary:
Windows 11 users should avoid unnecessary alarm when viewing Event Viewer logs, as many recorded errors and warnings are routine system processes rather than signs of critical hardware failure.

### Key Points
- Event Viewer categorizes logs into Information, Warning, Error, and Critical tiers to track system activity.
- Most Error and Warning messages represent routine background retries or minor configuration checks that do not impact daily performance.
- Critical errors typically indicate severe system crashes, such as a Blue Screen of Death, and are the primary logs requiring investigation.
- Reliability Monitor and BlueScreenView offer more user-friendly interfaces for diagnosing system stability compared to the standard Event Viewer.
- Event Viewer is intended as a reactive troubleshooting tool for existing problems rather than a proactive maintenance dashboard for healthy computers.

### Why it Matters
Misinterpreting routine system logs can lead users to perform unnecessary troubleshooting or worry about non-existent PC issues. Understanding that Event Viewer is a diagnostic tool for active problems helps users focus on genuine system failures while ignoring harmless background activity.

Advisory at a Glance
| Title | #StopRansomware: SafePay Ransomware | 
|---|---|
| Original Publication | October 20, 2026 | 
| Executive Summary | This advisory details recent activity by the SafePay ransomware group. SafePay actors have been highly active since August 2024, targeting businesses and critical infrastructure across North America, South America, Europe, and Australia. SafePay actors typically gain access to networks by stealing or guessing passwords, exploiting vulnerabilities in security systems, and using phishing tactics. Once inside the network, SafePay actors establish control by creating new accounts or taking over existing ones. They then use legitimate system tools to move through the network, identify valuable files, and disable security protections to avoid detection. Following, they encrypt the victim’s files, making them inaccessible, and leave a ransom note demanding payment in cryptocurrency. This advisory urges organizations to follow recommended security measures to reduce the risk and impact of SafePay ransomware attacks. | 
| Affected Products |  | 
| Key Actions |  | 
| Indicators of Compromise | For a downloadable copy of indicators of compromise, see: | 
| Intended Audience | Organizations: Government; Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB); State, Local, Tribal, and Territorial (SLTT); Critical Infrastructure Roles: Defensive cybersecurity analysts, vulnerability analysts, security systems managers, and operational technology (OT) owners and operators | 
Introduction
Note: This joint Cybersecurity Advisory is part of an ongoing #StopRansomware effort to publish advisories for network defenders that detail various ransomware variants and ransomware threat actors. These #StopRansomware advisories include recently and historically observed tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) and indicators of compromise (IOCs) to help organizations protect against ransomware. Visit stopransomware.gov to see all #StopRansomware advisories and to learn more about other ransomware threats and no-cost resources.
The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), United States Secret Service (USSS), Germany’s Landeskriminalamt Rheinland-Pfalz, the United Kingdom’s National Crime Agency, and the United Kingdom’s North West Regional Organised Crime Unit—hereafter referred to as the authoring agencies—are releasing this joint advisory to disseminate known SafePay ransomware TTPs and IOCs identified through FBI, USSS, and Landeskriminalamt Rheinland-Pfalz investigations as recently as August 2026.
Since August 2024, SafePay ransomware group’s operations have affected a wide range of businesses and critical infrastructure in North America, South America, Europe, and Australia. SafePay ransomware was among the most active ransomware groups in 2026. The SafePay threat actors have impacted at least 600 separate victims from multiple critical infrastructure sectors.
The authoring agencies encourage organizations to implement the recommendations in the Mitigations section of this advisory to reduce the likelihood and impact of SafePay ransomware incidents.
Download the PDF version of this report:
For a downloadable copy of IOCs, see:
Technical Details
Note: This advisory uses the MITRE ATT&CK® Matrix for Enterprise framework, version 20. See MITRE ATT&CK Tactics and Techniques section of this advisory for a table of the threat actors’ activity mapped to MITRE ATT&CK tactics and techniques.
Initial Access
The FBI, USSS, and cybersecurity researchers observed SafePay threat actors obtaining initial access [TA0001] to organizations through various means, including credential exposure, implementing brute force password attacks [T1110], and exploiting virtual private network (VPN) access. SafePay threat actors use the IP addresses of the VPN provider “Mullvad” to attain initial access—specifically, SafePay threat actors use phished account profiles to access victim networks to exploit the following known Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) for edge device products:
- CVE-2020-3259 [Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE)-200: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor]
- CVE-2023-20269 [CWE-288: Authentication Bypass Using an Alternate Path or Channel]
Additionally, the authoring agencies observed SafePay threat actors exploiting the following vulnerabilities across internet-exposed systems [T1190] for initial access through automated scripts:
Execution, Persistence, Stealth, and Defense Impairment
After SafePay threat actors gain access to a victim network, they establish persistence by gaining administrative privileges on existing accounts [T1098], or on newly created accounts [T1136], using built-in administrative tools consistent with living off the land (LOTL) techniques. Once SafePay threat actors establish a foothold in a victim’s network, they use LOTL binaries (LOLBins) [T1218], such as PsExec [T1021.002] and Windows Remote Management (WinRM) [T1021.006], to execute commands on remote systems. In several instances, SafePay threat actors used ShareFinder.ps1—a PowerShell script function used for enumerating network file shares in Windows Active Directory environments—to identify valuable assets for exfiltration [T1059.001, T1059.003]. Additionally, SafePay threat actors used SharpShares.exe, a tool used to identify and enumerate network file shares.
As SafePay threat actors prepare for lateral movement, they commonly disable security software [T1685] to avoid detection. In some cases, the threat actors changed the passwords of system users, making valid logins impossible. SafePay threat actors have also been observed using software packing or virtual machine software protection to conceal their code [T1027.002].
Privilege Escalation
The authoring agencies observed SafePay threat actors using a User Account Control (UAC) Bypass Privilege Escalation technique [T1548.002] that creates an elevated process through a specified component object model, enabling the execution of malicious commands or binaries [T1059]. SafePay threat actors have also been observed using token impersonation methods [T1134.001].
Lateral Movement
To pivot laterally through a network and identify files for exfiltration [TA0010] and encryption, SafePay threat actors use legitimate tools like PsExec, WinRM, and Remote Management and Monitoring [T1569.002] software. They also employ Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) [T1021.001, T1133] to expand their presence within the compromised network [T1021]. As SafePay threat actors move laterally through a network, they look for credentials to gain admin access and will create accounts, if needed.
Collection, Exfiltration, and Impact
SafePay threat actors use legitimate tools, such as FileZilla, 7-Zip, RClone, and WinRAR to compress files and collect data [T1560.001], and WinSCP and RClone to facilitate the exfiltration of data [T1048] from the compromised network to actor-controlled accounts. In some instances, SafePay threat actors use OneDrive to exfiltrate data [T1567]. In other instances, the SafePay threat actors installed legitimate remote desktop tools like AnyDesk or TeamViewer on the victim’s systems. SafePay threat actors use these tools to transfer ransomware and other software onto a victim’s system. Additionally, SafePay threat actors halt the Volume Shadow Copy Service and reset Network Attached Storage containing victim backup data to initial factory settings to inhibit system recovery attempts [T1490].
Following exfiltration, SafePay threat actors encrypt files [T1486] using a sophisticated hybrid encryption scheme to lock data. This involves combining a ChaCha20 stream cipher with an RSA public-key cryptosystem for a fast and secure key exchange. This multilayered approach customizes encryption methods based on file type and size and enables full or partial encryption. Data encrypted with the SafePay ransomware variant (appended with .SafePay) cannot be recovered without the decryption key. SafePay threat actors hold the encrypted data for ransom and typically demand a subset of company revenue in cryptocurrency in exchange for decryption software. SafePay threat actors leave a ransom note on the victim’s system, typically on the desktop or root directory, advising them that SafePay locked their system and to reach out over a chat portal at a TOR .onion website link with a victim ID as the login. To put pressure on the victim, a representative makes phone calls on behalf of the ransomware group. If the victim does not pay, SafePay posts the exfiltrated data to their SafePay leak website, which is linked in the ransom note. Following encryption, SafePay may delete itself from the victim’s filesystem [T1070.004].
Leveraged Tools
Table 1 lists publicly available tools and applications used by SafePay threat actors, including legitimate tools repurposed for their operations.
Note: These tools and applications should not be attributed as malicious without analytical evidence to support threat actor use and/or control.

| 7-Zip | An open source software that enables users to compress various file formats. SafePay threat actors maliciously use 7-Zip for data packaging and movement. | 
| FileZilla | An open source client that enables users to transfer files between servers. SafePay threat actors use FileZilla maliciously for data exfiltration. | 
| Mimikatz | A credential dumper that enables users to view and save authentication credentials, such as Kerberos tickets [T1550.002]. SafePay threat actors use Mimikatz for password exfiltration. | 
| PowerShell | A cross-platform task automation solution used for various malicious activities, including command execution. It is composed of a command-line shell, a scripting language, and a configuration management framework—which runs on Windows, Linux, and macOS. |

| ScreenConnect | A remote support, access, and meeting software that allows users to control devices remotely over the internet. SafePay threat actors use ScreenConnect for persistence and access. | 
| ShareFinder.ps1 | A PowerShell script used to scan an Active Directory network for shared folders. SafePay threat actors use ShareFinder.ps1 for exfiltration hunting. |

Incident Response
If a potential compromise is detected, but ransomware actors have not (yet) encrypted items, organizations should take the following actions:
- Determine which hosts were compromised and isolate them by quarantining or taking them offline.
- Initiate threat hunting activities to scope the intrusion. Collect and review relevant artifacts, logs, and other data to identify threat actor TTPs, compromised devices and accounts, a timeline of activity, etc.
- Report the suspected compromise to the FBI and other agencies as appropriate (if located within the U.K., report the compromise to Report Fraud or local police force) (see the Reporting section for contact information).
- Apply eviction countermeasures, including those listed below, to contain the incident and eradicate the threat actor from the network (Note: Start applying countermeasures after collecting enough threat hunting data to inform effective countermeasure selection; this will likely overlap with threat hunting activities). 
  - Use CISA’s Eviction Strategies Tool to assemble countermeasures for a systematic eviction plan—the tool comprises Playbook-NG (a web application) and COUN7ER (a database of post-compromise countermeasures mapped to adversary TTPs). 
    - Use Playbook-NG and COUN7ER together to assemble a systematic eviction plan, or playbook, that leverages distinct countermeasures to contain and evict cyber threat actors. The playbook features a list of recommended response actions based on threat actor TTPs and includes each action’s intended outcome, preparatory steps, and associated risks. For more information, see CISA’s Eviction Strategies Tool fact sheet.
- Harden the network to prevent additional malicious activity (see Mitigations for guidance).
If compromise is detected and items have been encrypted, see the “Ransomware and Data Extortion Response Checklist” in CISA’s joint #StopRansomware Guide.
The authoring agencies recommend organizations implement the mitigations below to improve their cybersecurity posture on the basis of the threat actors’ activity. These mitigations align with the Cross-Sector Cybersecurity Performance Goals (CPGs) developed by CISA and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). The CPGs provide a minimum set of practices and protections that CISA and NIST recommend all organizations implement. CISA and NIST based the CPGs on existing cybersecurity frameworks and guidance to protect against the most common and impactful threats, tactics, techniques, and procedures. Visit CISA’s CPGs webpage for more information on the CPGs, including additional recommended baseline protections.
Organizations should implement the following mitigations:
- Prioritize remediating known exploited vulnerabilities (KEVs) and keep all operating systems, software, and firmware up to date, as timely patching is one of the most efficient and cost-effective steps an organization can take to minimize its exposure to cybersecurity threats; specifically, prioritize patching KEVs in internet-facing systems. [CPG 2.B].
  - Additionally, using Binding Operational Directive 26-04 offers a framework for patch prioritization based on technology type and steps for forensics triage. Under its implementation guidance, it offers guidance and steps to perform forensic triage for severe vulnerability cases.
- Implement identity, credential, and access management (ICAM) policies across the organization and require MFA for all services to the greatest extent possible—particularly for webmail, VPNs, and accounts that access critical systems [CPG 3.F].
- Require all accounts with password logins (e.g., service accounts, admin accounts, and domain admin accounts) to comply with NIST’s digital identity guidelines; require employees to use long passwords and consider not requiring recurring password changes, as these can weaken security [CPG 3.B].
  - Use longer passwords consisting of at least 15 characters and no more than 64 characters in length.
  - Store passwords in a hashed format using industry-recognized password managers.
  - Add password user “salts” to shared login credentials.
  - Avoid reusing passwords [CPG 3.C].
  - Implement multiple failed login attempt account lockouts [CPG 3.E].
  - Disable password “hints.”
  - Refrain from requiring password changes more frequently than once per year.
Note: NIST guidance suggests favoring longer passwords instead of requiring frequent password resets. Frequent password resets are more likely to result in users developing password patterns cyber threat actors can easily decipher.
- Maintain offline backups of data and regularly test and maintain backup and restoration processes [CPG 3.O]; implementing this practice helps organizations avoid severe operational interruptions and prevents scenarios in which data is irretrievable.
- Ensure all backup data is encrypted, immutable (i.e., cannot be altered or deleted), and covers the entire organization’s data infrastructure [CPG 3.K].
- Implement a recovery plan to maintain and retain multiple copies of sensitive or proprietary data and servers in a physically separate, segmented, and secure location (e.g., hard drives, storage devices, or the cloud) [CPG 3.I, 3.O, 1.C].
- Segment networks to prevent the spread of ransomware, as network segmentation can help control traffic flows between, and access to, various subnetworks and restrict adversary lateral movement [CPG 3.I].
- Identify, detect, and investigate abnormal activity and potential traversal of the indicated ransomware with a network monitoring tool [CPG 4.B].
  - To aid in detecting ransomware, implement a tool that logs and reports all network traffic, including lateral movement activity on a network.
  - Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) tools are particularly useful for detecting lateral connections as they have insight into common and uncommon network connections for each host.
- Filter network traffic by preventing unknown or untrusted origins from accessing remote services on internal systems—this prevents threat actors from directly connecting to remote access services that they have established for persistence.
- Review domain controllers, servers, workstations, and Active Directories for new, unactive and/or unrecognized accounts.
- Disable unused ports.
- Consider adding an email banner to emails received from outside of your organization.
- Audit user accounts with administrative privileges and configure access controls according to the principle of least privilege [CPG 3.G].
- Implement time-based access for accounts set at the admin level and higher; for example, the Just-in-Time (JIT) access method provisions privileged access when needed and can support enforcement of the principle of least privilege (as well as the Zero Trust Maturity Model).
  - This is a process where a network-wide policy is set in place to automatically disable admin accounts at the Active Directory level when the account is not in direct need.
  - Individual users may submit their requests through an automated process that grants them access to a specified system for a set timeframe when they need to support the completion of a certain task.
- Disable command-line and scripting activities and permissions, since privilege escalation and lateral movement often depend on software utilities running from the command line; if threat actors cannot run these tools, they will have difficulty escalating privileges and moving laterally [CPG 3.M].
These mitigations align with principles provided in the joint guide Shifting the Balance of Cybersecurity Risk: Principles and Approaches for Secure by Design Software. CISA urges software manufacturers to take ownership of improving the security outcomes of their customers by applying these and other secure by design tactics. By implementing secure by design tactics, software manufacturers can make their product lines secure “out of the box” without requiring customers to make additional configuration changes, purchasing product security add-in software and logs, monitoring, and making frequent security updates.
Validate Security Controls
In addition to applying mitigations, the authoring agencies recommend exercising, testing, and validating your organization's security program against the threat behaviors mapped to the MITRE ATT&CK for Enterprise framework in this advisory.
To get started:
- Select an ATT&CK technique described in this advisory (see Table 6 to Table 16).
- Align your security technologies against the technique.
- Test your technologies against the technique.
- Analyze your detection and prevention technologies’ performance.
- Repeat the process for all security technologies to obtain a set of comprehensive performance data.
- Tune your security program, including people, processes, and technologies, based on the data generated by this process.
The authoring agencies recommend continually testing your security program, at scale, in a production environment to ensure optimal performance against the MITRE ATT&CK techniques identified in this advisory.
Resources
- Stopransomware.gov is a whole-of-government approach that provides one central location for ransomware resources and alerts.
- CISA’s #StopRansomware Guide provides organizations with comprehensive best practices to mitigate the risk of ransomware attacks.
- CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog is an authoritative resource for organizations to support improvement of their patch management best practices.
- CISA’s Multifactor Authentication webpage provides best practices for network defenders to mitigate threats to accounts and systems that use MFA.
- CISA’s Cyber Hygiene Services help organizations reduce the risk of a successful cyberattack.
- USSS’s Preparing for a Cyber Incident outlines basic steps an organization can take before, during, and after a cyber incident.
- CISA’s Cyber Security Evaluation Tool (CSET) provides a systematic, disciplined, and repeatable approach for evaluating an organization’s security posture; see Downloading and Installing CSET for step-by-step guidance to help your organization evaluate cybersecurity practices on your networks.
- CISA’s Ransomware Risk Assessment helps assess an organization’s ability to counteract a ransomware infection.
- Department of Health and Human Services’ Cybersecurity Performance Goals is a resource to help healthcare organizations implement high-impact cybersecurity practices.
- CISA’s Binding Operational Directive 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk and its implementation guidance
- CISA’s CI Fortify: Strengthening Resilience Across Critical Infrastructure
- CISA’s Eviction Strategies Tool enables incident response teams to quickly turn observed behaviors into remediation plans
- U.K.’s National Cyber Security Centre
- U.K.’s National Crime Agency
Your organization has no obligation to respond or provide information to the FBI and other authoring agencies in response to this joint advisory. If, after reviewing the information provided, your organization decides to provide information to the FBI or other authoring agencies, reporting must be consistent with applicable state and federal laws.
The FBI and other authoring agencies are interested in any information, to include boundary logs showing communication to and from foreign IP addresses, a sample ransom note, communications with threat actors, Bitcoin wallet information, decryptor files, and/or a benign sample of an encrypted file.
Additional details of interest include a targeted company point of contact, status and scope of infection, estimated loss, operational impact, transaction IDs, date of infection, date detected, initial attack vector, and host- and network-based indicators.
The authoring agencies do not encourage paying ransom as payment does not guarantee victim files will be recovered. Furthermore, payment may also embolden adversaries to target additional organizations, encourage other criminal actors to engage in the distribution of ransomware, and/or fund illicit activities. Regardless of whether you or your organization have decided to pay the ransom, the FBI and CISA urge you to promptly report ransomware incidents to the FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3), a local FBI field office, a local USSS Field Office, or CISA via the agency’s Incident Reporting System or its 24/7 Operations Center (contact@cisa.dhs.gov) or by calling 1-844-Say-CISA (1-844-729-2472).
In the U.K., report incidents of a cybercrime or fraud at the UK’s Home for Reporting Cyber Crime & Fraud or 0300-123-2040, your local police force, or use the non-emergency number 101.

The authoring agencies recognize that infrastructure used for malicious activity may be hosted on cloud or virtualized platforms where IP addresses can be dynamically or temporarily assigned. As a result, an address associated with malicious activity at one point in time may later be reassigned to benign services. Accordingly, these indicators should be interpreted as historically observed infrastructure within the activity window and should be corroborated with current network telemetry or additional intelligence sources when used for defensive or investigative purposes.
