SafePay ransomware has targeted over 600 businesses and critical infrastructure organizations globally since August 2024, utilizing credential theft, phishing, and system vulnerabilities to encrypt sensitive data for ransom.

### Key Points
- SafePay actors gain initial network access by exploiting VPN vulnerabilities, brute-forcing passwords, and using phished account profiles.
- The group employs "living off the land" techniques, using legitimate administrative tools like PsExec and WinRM to move laterally and disable security software.
- Data is exfiltrated using common utilities such as RClone, FileZilla, and cloud services like OneDrive before files are encrypted with a hybrid RSA/ChaCha20 scheme.
- Ransom demands are typically issued in cryptocurrency, with threats to publish stolen data on a dedicated leak site if payments are not met.
- Authoring agencies, including the FBI and CISA, have identified specific indicators of compromise, including malicious IP addresses and custom PowerShell scripts like ShareFinder.ps1.

### Why it Matters
This advisory highlights a significant threat to global critical infrastructure, emphasizing the need for robust identity management and network segmentation to prevent widespread operational disruption. Organizations must prioritize patching known vulnerabilities and maintaining immutable, offline backups to mitigate the severe financial and data-loss risks posed by this active ransomware group.

results.title: Release Of ‘GTA VI’ Will Cost American Companies A Fortune According To Professor Who Calculated Economic Impact
results.author: Connor Toole
results.content:
We’re a month away from the release of Grand Theft Auto VI, which is probably the most highly anticipated video game of all time. There’s no way to know how many Americans will skip work to play it, but an economics professor attempted to figure that out while forecasting a massive hit for the companies that will have to deal with their absence.
It’s been close to 4,800 days since the release of Grand Theft Auto V, which has become the most profitable entertainment product ever released since the most recent installment of the wildly popular video game franchise came out on September 17, 2013.
That title dropped players into an updated version of San Andreas five years after the previous one transported them back to Liberty City, but fans hoping for the next follow-up have been forced to endure a more than 13-year wait that will finally come to an end when Grand Theft Auto VI finally drops on November 19th of this year.
Based on Rockstar’s reputation (along with the footage and early reviews we’ve been treated to so far), it’s very, very hard to imagine that it’s not going to live up to the virtually unprecedented amount of hype surrounding it.
The fact that GTA VI is coming out on a Thursday is less than ideal for people who work a typical job, as they’ll have to wait until the weekend rolls around to truly dive into the world of Leonida. However, those who opt to schedule some time off or call in “sick” have the potential to collectively cost their employers a significant chunk of change.
An economics professor believes 1.5 million people will miss work to play GTA VI and be responsible for $1 billion in lost productivity
Some employers are very aware of the impact GTA VI is poised to have on their workers.
Over the summer, a company in California opted to wave the white flag by preemptively scaling back operations on release day, and the head of an Army battalion stationed in Georgia dangled a four-day pass that coincides with the debut to try to boost reenlistments.
According to the International Business Times, José García Montalvo, a professor of economics at Pompeu Fabra University in Barcelona, Spain, attempted to figure out just how costly the release of GTA VI will be to the American economy, and he settled on a ten-figure sum after crunching the numbers.
Montalvo estimates 1.5 million people in the United States will skip out on work to play the game on the 19th, noting most of them will fall in the 18 to 30 range and asserting the tech industry will be disproportionately impacted by absences.
He pegged the average salary at $70,000, and if the 2% productivity dip he forecasts is correct, GTA VI will end up costing the companies they work for around $1 billion in a single day.
GTA VI isn’t the only form of entertainment with the ability to have an impact on that scale; March Madness is responsible for an even bigger number, as the NCAA Tournament was thought to be the root of around $12 billion worth of lost productivity this year.
results.summary:
Rockstar Games is set to release Grand Theft Auto VI on November 19, with economic forecasts predicting that 1.5 million Americans may skip work to play the highly anticipated title.

### Key Points
- Grand Theft Auto VI launches on November 19, ending a 13-year wait since the release of its predecessor.
- Economics professor José García Montalvo estimates the game will cause $1 billion in lost productivity across the United States.
- Approximately 1.5 million employees, primarily aged 18 to 30, are expected to miss work to play the game upon its release.
- The technology sector is projected to face the most significant impact from employee absences on the launch date.
- Some employers are preemptively adjusting operations or offering incentives to manage the anticipated workforce disruption.

### Why it Matters
The massive scale of this release highlights the significant influence major entertainment products now exert on national labor productivity and corporate operations. While the $1 billion impact is substantial, it remains smaller than the estimated $12 billion in lost productivity attributed annually to the NCAA March Madness tournament.

results.title: Hackers Exploit Plex2Shell Flaws to Install Crypto Miners and Linux Proxy Backdoor
results.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
results.content:
Threat actors have begun to exploit a chain of vulnerabilities in Plex Media Server to deploy cryptocurrency miners and reverse proxy software, a day after a proof-of-concept (PoC) went public.
According to a researcher who goes by the online alias boredhackerblog, the exploitation activity involves chaining four different vulnerabilities, collectively called Plex2Shell.
The vulnerabilities are below -
- CVE-2026-96652 (CVSS score: 5.3) - An unauthenticated server-side request forgery (SSRF) stemming via the "/player/timeline" endpoint by taking advantage of the fact that the "protocol" parameter is inserted into a programmatically-constructed player URL with no validation, allowing an attacker to force the Plex server to POST to a destination of their choice.
- CVE-2026-96654 (CVSS score: 6.9) - An improper neutralization of URL values included in the "searchOne" endpoint that could allow an attacker to call other plugins' functions and supply their own parameters to obtain the owner's admin token.
- CVE-2026-96655 (CVSS score: 5.3) - An SSRF vulnerability that allows an authenticated user (i.e., the owner token) to request arbitrary internal or external addresses (e.g., an attacker-hosted carrier video carrying the malicious ELF payload) via the '/video/:/transcode/universal' path parameter.
- CVE-2026-96656 (CVSS score: 8.6) - An external control of file name or path vulnerability that writes the ELF shared object to an attacker-chosen path in the Codecs directory and execute it.
Put differently, the vulnerabilities can be combined together in this order to achieve unauthenticated remote code execution on susceptible Plex Media Server instances.
The vulnerabilities, along with CVE-2026-96651 (CVSS score: 7.1), were disclosed to Plex on July 27, 2026, by security researcher Zach Main, and were patched in Plex Media Server 1.43.3.10861 released on August 3, 2026.
In-the-wild exploitation attempts targeting the flaws have since been recorded a day after technical details of the Plex2Shell chain went public on October 16, 2026. The attacks make use of a shell script to retrieve and deploy a miner payload ("x12345") hosted on a remote server ("217.60.194[.]116") using wget or curl.
The attack efforts have been observed from the following IP addresses -
- 91.92.40[.]202
- 176.65.139[.]228
- 45.194.92[.]222
- 176.65.139[.]228
| The Plex2Shell chain \| Source: Zach Main | 
Furthermore, the vulnerabilities have been exploited to deliver an artifact named "myawesomeproxy," which, according to VirusTotal, is a stealthy Linux backdoor and reverse proxy. Running the program displays the below message, per boredhackerblog -
Running this software on any of your devices makes you agree to the potential external use of your internet traffic.
Also deployed concurrently is an XMRig miner process identified as "mylovelyminer" with its mining server pointing to "ota.proxystream[.]st." Notably, another subdomain associated with the same domain, "global.relay.proxystream[.]st," was flagged by Bitsight in August 2026 in connection with the AISURU DDoS and proxyware botnet.
Posts on Reddit indicate that multiple Plex users have had their instances compromised with the same "mylovelyminer" payload. That said, it's not known at this stage if it stems from the exploitation of Plex2Shell flaws.
The development comes more than a month after Plex urged users to update their instances to the latest version following the release of an update that addressed multiple unspecified security flaws.
It's unclear if the aforementioned vulnerabilities were part of this alert. The Hacker News has contacted Plex for comment and we will update the story if we hear back. In light of active exploitation, users are advised to keep their Plex installations up-to-date for optimal protection.
results.summary:
Threat actors are actively exploiting a chain of four vulnerabilities, collectively known as Plex2Shell, to deploy cryptocurrency miners and reverse proxy software on vulnerable Plex Media Server instances.

### Key Points
- The Plex2Shell exploit chain allows unauthenticated remote code execution by chaining four vulnerabilities, including CVE-2026-96656, which carries a high CVSS score of 8.6.
- Security researcher Zach Main disclosed the flaws on July 27, 2026, and Plex released a patch in version 1.43.3.10861 on August 3, 2026.
- Attackers are using the exploit to install the "mylovelyminer" XMRig payload and a Linux backdoor identified as "myawesomeproxy."
- Malicious activity has been traced to several IP addresses, including 91.92.40.202 and 45.194.92.222, following the public release of proof-of-concept code on October 16, 2026.
- Users are urged to update their Plex installations immediately to mitigate the risk of unauthorized remote access and resource hijacking.

### Why it Matters
This exploit chain poses a significant security risk to home media server users by enabling attackers to gain full control over compromised systems. Promptly updating software is essential to prevent the unauthorized deployment of botnet-related proxies and cryptocurrency mining operations that can degrade system performance and compromise network security.

results.title: The Metric Is Not The Mission: When The Reckoning Reaches The Courts
results.author: Konstantinos Komaitis
results.content:
The Metric Is Not The Mission: When The Reckoning Reaches The Courts
The Metric Is Not the Mission is a ten-part examination of how Big Tech moved from building and expanding the open internet to increasingly shaping it around its own metrics, incentives and assumptions. Across the series, the argument follows the evolution of the platform economy—from the optimism of the early internet to the growing tensions around power, prediction, geopolitics, accountability and the future of digital life.
The series will be published in two parts each week over five weeks, with each installment building on the one before it. At the end of the series, the complete essay will be brought together in a single PDF edition, providing the full argument in one place.
Part IX — When the Reckoning Reaches the Courts 
Part VIII questioned whether regulation alone can alter the balance of power between Big Tech and society. Part IX asks what happens when accountability moves beyond legislation and into the courts and users themselves begin to demand answers.
There is a revealing assumption embedded in much of the debate about Big Tech: that the companies will eventually reform because political pressure, public criticism, and increasingly sophisticated regulation will persuade them to do so. Perhaps. But history suggests a less charitable and probably more realistic explanation for corporate change.
Powerful companies rarely abandon profitable business models because they have suddenly concluded that those models are incompatible with the public interest. They do so when the legal, financial or reputational costs of maintaining them become impossible to ignore. The tobacco industry did not transform because it discovered the importance of public health. Financial institutions did not fundamentally rethink their practices because criticism alone persuaded them that markets required greater responsibility. In industry after industry, public pressure mattered enormously, but the decisive moment often arrived when pressure acquired legal consequences.
That may be where Big Tech is now heading. For years, the debate surrounding the platforms was framed primarily as a regulatory problem. Were governments moving fast enough? Were legislators sufficiently technologically literate? Should companies be treated as publishers, utilities, common carriers, or something else entirely? What new obligations should be imposed upon recommendation systems, advertising models, app stores, artificial intelligence or the collection of personal data?
Those questions remain important. But there is another question beginning to emerge beneath them: what happens when users stop waiting for governments to solve the problem and begin asking courts whether the companies themselves can be held accountable?
This changes the nature of the debate. Legislation generally operates prospectively. It tells companies what they must do in the future. Courts can also look backwards. They ask what happened, who knew, what could reasonably have been anticipated and whether an organization’s choices contributed to a particular harm. That is a much more uncomfortable form of accountability.
A company can lobby against a bill. It can seek changes to legislation before it is passed. It can influence regulatory guidance and negotiate implementation. None of this guarantees success, but large corporations have spent decades developing the institutional machinery required to participate effectively in the political process.
Courts are different. Once a legal dispute has reached the question of responsibility, the argument is no longer only about what policymakers might require in the abstract. It becomes a question about evidence. Internal documents. Design decisions. Warnings. Risk assessments. Corporate knowledge. The relationship between what a company knew and what it chose to do.
The burden of explanation begins to shift. For the platforms, that shift may prove more consequential than another round of hearings in Washington or Brussels. The first major test of this new pressure may be child safety and there are obvious reasons why.
Few questions are as politically powerful as the safety of children. Abstract arguments about freedom of expression, innovation, and technological progress become considerably more difficult when confronted with evidence that children may be exposed to foreseeable and preventable harm. The question changes from whether a platform is generally beneficial to society to whether a company knew that particular features, systems or incentives created specific risks for vulnerable users and failed to take reasonable action.
That is not merely a regulatory question; it is a question of responsibility. And it may become the point at which the existing model of platform governance begins to change.
Yet child safety cannot be the end of the story. Indeed, it would be a mistake to treat children as the only people whose relationship with digital platforms deserves meaningful protection. Children may provide the clearest and most politically compelling case, but the deeper principle is broader. Adults also deserve protection from business models designed around asymmetries of information and power. Users also have interests in privacy, autonomy, and agency. Citizens also have interests in digital environments that do not systematically exploit vulnerabilities merely because those vulnerabilities can be measured and monetized. Communities also have interests in systems that do not treat social cohesion as collateral damage in the pursuit of engagement. And society as a whole has an interest in ensuring that the companies which increasingly mediate its public life cannot simply define responsibility according to the limits of what legislation has explicitly prohibited.
This is the larger reckoning. The argument is not that technology companies are uniquely evil; nor is it that every social problem produced online can be traced to corporate malice. That is neither accurate nor particularly useful.
The platforms built extraordinary technologies. They solved real problems. They connected people across distances that previous generations could barely imagine. Their success was deserved, at least in part, because they made the internet more accessible, more useful, and more powerful.
The question is what happens when the institutions that produced those achievements become sufficiently powerful that their own understanding of responsibility becomes one of the principal constraints on their power. For too long, the answer has been: very little. Platforms investigated themselves. Companies commissioned their own research. Executives appeared before legislatures. Regulators announced new inquiries. Governments threatened action. And the underlying model continued largely unchanged.
This is why the current moment may be different. The reckoning will not come because Big Tech has suddenly come to Jesus. It will not come because the companies have collectively discovered that human flourishing is a better objective than engagement. Nor will it come simply because legislators have finally written sufficiently strict rules, although legislation can and should play a crucial role in establishing the boundaries within which digital power operates.
The more profound change will come when Big Tech no longer controls the terms of the conversation about the harms it creates. That is what users and courts can do. Users can withdraw the legitimacy that platforms have long assumed their scale provides. They can demand alternatives, organize and bring claims. They can transform the experience of harm from an abstract policy problem into a question of accountability.
Courts, in the meantime, can ask questions that corporate public relations and political lobbying are designed to avoid. What did the company know? When did it know it? What did it do with that knowledge? Were risks foreseeable? Were warnings ignored? Was a particular outcome simply an unfortunate consequence of innovation, or was it connected to choices that could reasonably have been made differently?
These questions are more difficult to absorb into a compliance department. They may also prove more difficult to solve through lobbying.
Konstantinos Komaitis, PhD, is a veteran of developing and analysing Internet policy to ensure an open and global Internet.

results.summary:
The ninth installment of the "Metric Is Not the Mission" series examines how litigation and judicial accountability may force Big Tech to reform beyond traditional legislative efforts.

### Key Points
- The series argues that Big Tech companies rarely change profitable business models unless faced with significant legal, financial, or reputational consequences.
- Unlike prospective legislation, court proceedings focus on retrospective evidence, internal corporate knowledge, and specific design decisions regarding user harm.
- Child safety is identified as the primary catalyst for this shift, as it forces platforms to defend specific features against claims of foreseeable harm.
- The author suggests that moving accountability into the courts shifts the burden of explanation away from lobbyists and toward internal corporate documentation.
- Broader societal interests, including privacy, autonomy, and social cohesion, are presented as the next frontiers for potential legal challenges against platform power.

### Why it Matters
This shift toward litigation represents a fundamental change in how digital platforms are held accountable for their business practices. By moving beyond lobbying and regulatory compliance, courts can force companies to address the specific consequences of their design choices and internal knowledge.

results.title: Time Magazine Profiles John Ternus
results.author: John Gruber
results.content:
Just below the broad smile he’s been wearing all morning, John Ternus’ hands are shaking.
On this September day in Silicon Valley, Apple’s new CEO is surrounded by celebrities, tech enthusiasts, and reporters who have flocked to Apple Park from around the world to catch a glimpse of the company’s new and long-awaited foldable phone, the Duo. After Ternus takes a few photos with the device, an Apple PR rep pulls the influencer known as IShowSpeed out of the crowd to meet him. Winning over the 21-year-old isn’t exactly the toughest assignment Ternus has faced in his 25-year Apple career: Speed barks when he sees the phone and then gleefully springs into a backflip.
But IShowSpeed also happens to be livestreaming the encounter to his 61 million subscribers on YouTube. And as Ternus thumbs through the $1,999-and-up phone, attempting to drag a photo into a text-message box, eagle-eyed viewers notice his hands quivering. Ternus later explains that he didn’t sleep much the night before. “I was on such a moment of adrenaline and caffeine and excitement for the day,” he tells TIME.
Ternus, who took over as CEO on Sept. 1, was chosen to run Apple because he has ably applied his engineering and design expertise to shape products that redefined entire categories of technology, from the Mac to iPad to AirPods and the iPhone. But becoming the face and front man for the second biggest company in the world by market cap is another proposition entirely. Ternus’ hard technical skills may not translate easily to a position that involves toggling from Hollywood to stockholders, to politicians shaping policy, to rival CEOs in the constellation of tech companies whose power challenges nation-states.
His predecessor, Tim Cook, gained stature on the world stage as a power broker deftly navigating global politics, markets, and supply chains. Cook’s predecessor, Steve Jobs, was a rock-star visionary who sold the world on the deeply personal and even spiritual nature of tech creations. Ternus is different from both: a private, detail-oriented engineer, little known outside the company until he became a senior hardware executive in 2021.
Rather than try to replicate his forerunners’ styles of success, Ternus has so far played to his own strengths—which are also those of Apple, a company that first and foremost builds beautiful products that spark productivity, creativity, and joy. Ternus’ interaction with IShowSpeed is clearly designed to capture this (and, of course, to goose preorder numbers among the influencer’s young and massive audience). To some critics, however, the scene might read as a legacy company aura-farming to sell expensive gizmos instead of building the actual technological future, which is artificial intelligence.
Virtually every one of Apple’s fellow Goliaths—Microsoft, Google, Meta, Amazon, and now Nvidia, OpenAI, and Anthropic—have flung themselves into the AI arms race, pouring hundreds of billions of dollars into training ever more intelligent thinking machines. While Apple trains its own models, it is nowhere near the technology’s frontier, leaving the company vulnerable to being left behind if super-smart AI transforms industry and society in the coming years. At the end of September, Apple was conspicuously absent when President Donald Trump hosted a luncheon for AI power players like SpaceX’s Elon Musk, Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, and Google’s Sundar Pichai, who lobbied him on their visions for America’s tech future.
But Ternus and other Apple executives say they aren’t concerned. In the midst of a populist AI backlash, they contend that they are building a modest but personalized and privacy-preserving form of AI that will actually help ordinary people as opposed to merely dazzling Silicon Valley’s “lunatic fringe,” as Greg Joswiak, senior vice president of worldwide marketing, puts it. And besides, Ternus argues, even if other companies succeed in their mission of building super-intelligence, users will still want to talk to it on Apple devices.
“People want physical things,” he says a week later at the company’s flagship store on Fifth Avenue in New York City, wearing an amiable but guarded smile. He spent the morning greeting superfans who had lined up all night to get their hands on the iPhone 18. “They want to talk, to see images of loved ones, to take pictures. So I don’t see a scenario where all of a sudden, our devices disappear and we don’t have a need for an iPhone.”
Ternus is barely older than the company he’s running. Born in 1975 in Orange County—Apple was founded in ’76, just 400 miles north—he grew up as Steve Jobs was redefining the personal computer as a societal force. When Ternus was 8 years old, his father bought an Apple II. “I started playing games on it and fell in love with Apple,” he says. A decade later, he took his family’s newer Mac, an SE model, to college at the University of Pennsylvania, where he studied mechanical engineering.
In 2001, Ternus left a virtual reality company to join Apple at 26 as an engineer. He has now spent half his life at the company, rising through the ranks on his propensity to consider both how products are made and how the user will experience them. “John was really at the center of driving the spirit of collaboration across the company to make sure that end-to-end these products give you that delightful experience—and the technology kind of disappears as you’re using it,” says Richard Dinh, Apple’s vice president of product design.
Over the past 15 years, some critics have accused Apple of failing to innovate the way it did in previous eras, when the company popularized the home computer, the MP3 player, and the smartphone. But it is undeniable that Apple’s core products—its computers and phones—have remained elite thanks to behind-the-scenes innovations in hardware and software. And Ternus, Apple executives say, has been a big part of these improvements.
When Cook, 65, announced in April he would step down following a 15-year tenure, it was no surprise that the company tapped Ternus as his successor. Other executives describe him as pragmatic, meticulous, and unifying. “Ternus is a logical pick,” says Neil Cybart, an analyst who has been following Apple for more than a decade on his site Above Avalon. “He has been a big believer in this design-first culture that defines Apple, as well as the idea that it’s not just technology here; there needs to be something more.”
In the late 2010s, Apple executives shifted their messaging to focus more on fast-growing services like iCloud, the App Store, and Apple Music. But growth in service revenue has moderated this year, and the promotion of Ternus, a hardware and product guru, signals a return to the company’s roots.
So it’s fitting that his ascension coincided with the announcement of the Duo, Apple’s most radical design change to the iPhone since its 2007 release. Apple has been exploring the concept for years. In 2011, when many people still carried around flip phones, Ternus and five other engineers filed a patent application for foldable electronic devices, exploring what kind of batteries and circuit boards might be needed for such an idea. “It felt clear that we were going to eventually get to a place where OLED displays were going to be flexible,” Ternus says.
Many challenges stood in between the patent and the final product. The first attempts at a foldable smartphone in the 2010s from other companies tended to be fragile and not all that useful, with a big, ugly crease in the center interrupting the experience. “The other examples in the world felt kind of cheap and crappy,” Ternus says.
Across hardware and software teams, Apple engineers and designers got to work. With advancements in Apple silicon chips, they created a new display engine that facilitates seamless transitions between the inner and outer screens. They redesigned iOS to move the phone’s main controls from the bottom to the right side for easier thumb access.
Along the way, Ternus encouraged the team to invest more time and effort in the project, even as other foldables beat them to market. Dinh says that at one point, he asked Ternus whether his team should proceed with a top surface material similar to those of its competitors, which Dinh felt had flaws but was potentially good enough.
“And he was like, ‘Look, Rich, you’ll know when it’s the right thing.’ And that gave us the confidence to really push the boundaries on innovation and manufacturing, and fly worldwide to connect our suppliers together and come up with the nanotexture [a surface technology],” Dinh says. The result—a surface made from a custom polymer and built atop a hinge with more than 100 tiny interior precision components—has impressed its first users, who have said they can barely detect a crease at all.
Ultimately, the Duo promises a passport-size phone that opens into a powerful tablet. Users can stow it in their pockets, then open it up and watch a movie on its matte, light-deflecting surface. They can compare websites side by side, play touchscreen games with intricate detail, and use a dual-camera setup to simultaneously show themselves and what they’re seeing on FaceTime.
Of course, the Duo’s success is far from guaranteed. It could go the way of Apple flops like the Apple Car, which was never released, or the Vision Pro, which had staggeringly low sales in the last year. Certainly many prospective buyers will blanch at the device’s $2,000-plus price tag.
But the phone’s first public testers have given glowing feedback. And demand for the Duo’s closest rival, Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold8, has been strong, suggesting there is a growing appetite for the foldables category, especially in Asia.
Apple also hopes that the Duo will earn a cultural cachet among storytellers and other artists, many of whom, like loyal Apple customers, still regard the company more as a maker of useful tools rather than as the enemy Big Tech has become. Four-time Oscar winner Sean Baker (Anora), who spoke at a “no-AI” film festival earlier this year, attended the Duo announcement in Cupertino and described his relationship with Apple as collaborative. “It’s not just ‘buy or use our product’—it’s much more of a working relationship where they stay in touch and ask us for feedback,” he says.
Baker noted that Apple’s products often underpin many parts of the filmmaking process. For instance, when moviemakers need to add dialogue in postproduction, they often simply record on an iPhone, because it’s convenient and nearly production-grade.
In person, Ternus presents as a guy trying to blend in: he dresses in nondescript clothes and speaks in platitudes, often about the brilliance of Apple’s internal culture. He has devoted much of his early tenure as CEO to obsessing over design, spending multiple days a week in the studio with the industrial-design and human-interface teams.
But beyond Apple Park’s gleaming, curved walls, Ternus has tough choices to make. Case in point: the ongoing global shortage of memory chips, which has raised costs and delayed production timelines. In July, the Financial Times reported that Apple had begun testing memory chips made by a Chinese company as a way to increase supply. That drew a swift rebuke from a bipartisan group of Senators, who wrote a letter to Apple arguing that to do so would imperil national security.
Ternus pushes back on that idea. “The constraints in memory are absolutely a crisis,” he tells TIME in the second of two interviews during September. “So our fundamental belief is that all options should be on the table.”
Cook was skilled at managing relationships with governments around the world, vigorously defending Apple’s interests even if it made him a target of ridicule. His courtship of Trump, which included a widely maligned presentation of a disc with a 24-karat gold base at the White House in 2025, helped Apple secure relief from some of the Administration’s most punishing proposed levies.
Ternus is tight-lipped about how his approach to government affairs might differ from Cook’s. He says that he’s met with members of the Trump Administration to “make sure we’re kind of working through things together.” But as Ternus transitions into the role, Cook has continued to represent Apple on the world stage, meeting with Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, and then attending President Trump’s state dinner for Xi Jinping.
“He has great relationships and loves Apple,” Ternus says of Cook, who is staying on as Apple’s executive chairman. “So wherever he can help, he is happy to help.”
Big Tech has been hammered by lawsuits, public campaigns, and regulation over the past few years from critics who feel that screens have poisoned the cognitive development of an entire generation. From Australia and the U.K. to California and New York, governments have restricted children’s social media and AI use and phones in schools, while pressuring Apple and Google to build stronger protections into their devices.
Apple has traditionally framed many of these harms as arising from particular apps and content. But the company rolled out a redesigned Screen Time experience in September to give parents greater control over their children’s app access. Ternus pledges that child safety will be central to Apple’s approach going forward. He says that in the past, he used Apple’s Screen Time to monitor his kids’ device usage, and that it was “good but not great.” The company’s new updates, he says, stem from a desire “to build tools that make that really easy for parents—and I think we’ve done just that.”
Questions around geopolitical tensions, supply chains, and child safety only become more urgent as Apple wades into its next frontier: artificial intelligence.
Since the rise of ChatGPT in November 2022, the generative AI boom has unfolded with Apple largely sitting on the sidelines. OpenAI brought AI chatbots to the masses; Nvidia built the chips powering them. Microsoft, Google, Meta, Amazon, Anthropic, and SpaceX now all either compete at the technology’s frontier or are printing revenue from a key part of its supply chain.
Apple, in contrast, did not unveil Apple Intelligence until June 2024—18 months after ChatGPT’s release—and then spent more than two years struggling to deliver the personalized version of Siri it had promised. In 2025, realizing the existing Siri couldn’t grow into the AI era, the company scrapped it in favor of another version that had been two-tracked. The resulting new Siri, which launched in the U.S. in September, is powered by an Apple AI model that leverages Google’s Gemini technology. This arrangement puts Apple in an unusual position: reliant on a rival for a key building block of its products. This sort of outsourcing famously angered Jobs, who went to great lengths to own the “whole widget,” from hardware to software to services.
But Ternus rejects the idea that its AI strategy represents a retreat from that philosophy. After all, Apple relies on suppliers for many of its components, including screens, memory, and modems. “There’s not really a goal that we have to make every single thing in a product,” he says. “We make the things where we can really bring differentiation.”
Apple has said that AI is core to the company’s focus, and that it has significantly increased its investments in AI. The company also argues that the usefulness of AI comes less from its underlying raw power than what surrounds it—the chip it runs on, the operating system it inhabits, and the knowledge it has gathered about its user. The new Siri cannot code like OpenAI’s Codex or write as elegantly as Anthropic’s Claude. But with a user’s permission, it can draw connections across messages, emails, calendars, documents, and other information stored on Apple devices. It is designed to help prepare someone for a meeting, find a flight confirmation buried in an inbox, or help interpret health data collected by an Apple Watch.
“Everything in your life is on your phone,” Ternus says. “With Siri AI, you can leverage all that information to do things, learn things, and figure out things in a way that nobody else can do.”
Cybart, the analyst, argues that Apple has seen this kind of competition before. “People tend to think that if someone else does great, that must mean Apple has a problem, like in music or television streaming,” he says. “But how do you access Spotify or Netflix? When other companies do great things, that doesn’t change the fundamental story with Apple in terms of having the ecosystem that people want to be in.”
And Apple executives argue that some of Siri’s limitations are actually strengths. For instance, Siri’s lack of thinking power compared with other ultra-smart AI agents means that there’s far less of a chance of going rogue, or behaving in eerie ways. “We’ve purposely designed it not to be a companion, and we don’t want to replace human connection,” says Lilian Rincon, who leads Apple’s AI product efforts.
Privacy is another advantage Apple executives stress. The company has a decades-long reputation for protecting user data more aggressively than its competitors. Siri processes requests on-device where possible, and more computationally demanding asks are sent to Private Cloud Compute. Apple’s system of servers is designed so that queries are not stored or made available to the company. Apple has also made portions of that system inspectable by independent security researchers, some of whom have praised Apple’s approach while noting limits to its transparency.
Some investors are already treating Apple as a hedge against the other AI companies dominating the Nasdaq; if those companies wobble, Apple could be the big stock-market winner. Conversely, if AI progress continues apace, smaller but capable models could soon become able to run cheaply on devices built to handle them. In this future, the scarce asset would be not the chatbot, but the device, operating system, and personal context through which the chatbot becomes useful. And Apple has built a significant moat in the form of loyal customers across the world.
This thesis was already borne out earlier this year, when a wave of AI enthusiasts bought Mac Minis in order to set up personal AI agents through the open-source project OpenClaw.
While Apple had nothing to do with the project, users quickly figured out that the energy-efficient Apple silicon, compact form, and unified memory of the $600 computers allowed them to run AI workloads locally, continuously, and for minimal electricity costs. This spike in demand caused some Mac Mini models to be unavailable for months.
More AI-oriented hardware products are on the way. On Oct. 13, Apple announced a new smart-home hub called the HomeView, powered by Apple intelligence. Bloomberg also reported the company is readying smart glasses for 2027; the company declined to comment.
But Apple will soon face more competition in the hardware space. Last year, OpenAI acquired the startup of Jony Ive, Apple’s longtime chief design officer, who is now building AI-first devices for the ChatGPT maker alongside several other prominent former Apple veterans. In July, Apple sued OpenAI in federal court, alleging the theft of hardware trade secrets. (OpenAI calls the lawsuit “baseless.”)
Despite the lawsuit, Apple executives say they’re not worried about the newfound rivals. After all, Apple devices have never been more popular. With 2.5 billion active devices, the company rakes in nearly half a trillion dollars in annual revenue. And when new users convert to Apple, they tend to stick around. “We don’t feel threatened,” says Joswiak, the longtime executive. “The fact that we can do the integration that we can means we can create just a better experience than anybody else.”
Joswiak adds that Apple isn’t making products for the die-hard AI believers chasing superintelligence. “We love them, and they can use it too, but that’s not our target,” he says. “It’s how to make it better for everyday people.”
On Sept. 18, lines formed outside Apple stores from Hangzhou to London to Mumbai, with scores of those “everyday people” spending hundreds of their hard-earned dollars on the newest iPhone. Ternus, as Tim Cook and Steve Jobs did before him, showed up to the Fifth Avenue store to take pictures with superfans, who treated him like a movie star. Most of them probably didn’t know much about Ternus himself. But they didn’t need to, because they saw him -reflected through devices that had become omnipresent in their lives.
AI may yet be a part of their lives too. But no one knows the future—and at present, handheld devices are still king. “You can’t do everything,” Ternus says. “So we kind of try to constrain ourselves to the stuff that matters most—and then put all of our effort into those things.”

New Apple CEO John Ternus is navigating the company’s transition into the artificial intelligence era while launching the Duo, a high-end foldable smartphone designed to maintain Apple's hardware dominance.

### Key Points
- John Ternus officially became Apple CEO on September 1, succeeding Tim Cook after a 25-year career at the company.
- The newly released Duo foldable phone features a custom polymer surface and a precision hinge, marking Apple's most significant design shift since 2007.
- Apple is integrating Google’s Gemini technology into its new Siri to bolster AI capabilities while prioritizing on-device privacy and user data security.
- The company faces increased competition from AI-focused hardware startups, including a venture led by former Apple design chief Jony Ive.
- Apple currently maintains a massive ecosystem with 2.5 billion active devices, generating nearly $500 billion in annual revenue.

### Why it Matters
Apple is attempting to balance its traditional focus on premium hardware with the urgent need to remain relevant in a rapidly evolving artificial intelligence market. By emphasizing privacy-centric, personalized AI tools over general-purpose super-intelligence, the company aims to leverage its massive user base to maintain its competitive moat against tech rivals.
